L01 Agents, Multiagent Systems and Agentic AI

Exam questions

Give the Russell and Norvig and the Wooldridge definitions of an agent. What does each emphasise, and why do Russell and Norvig call the notion of an agent "a tool for analyzing systems"?

Key points: R&N: perceives environment through sensors, acts through actuators; Wooldridge: situated, autonomous action, design objectives; R&N stress the perception-action interface and “can be viewed as”, Wooldridge autonomy and goals; “agent” is a lens for analysis; calculator example.

Russell and Norvig: an agent is anything that can be viewed as perceiving its environment through sensors and acting upon it through actuators. Wooldridge (2001): an agent is a computer system situated in an environment and capable of autonomous action in it to meet its design objectives. Both place the agent in an observe-act loop with an environment. Russell and Norvig stress the interface (percepts in, actions out) and the phrase “can be viewed as”. Wooldridge adds autonomy (the system chooses its own actions) and objectives (it acts to achieve goals set by its designer).

Russell and Norvig warn that the notion of an agent is an analysis tool, not a line that divides the world into agents and non-agents. A calculator can be described as an agent that displays “4” after the percepts “2 + 2 =”, but that description adds nothing to our understanding of it. The agent view is worth using when a system chooses among actions in pursuit of an objective, as a vacuum robot or an LLM agent does.

Describe the kinds of agent program from simple reflex to learning agents. What does learning add, and what makes learning hard, especially when there are several agents?

Key points: simple reflex (current percept, condition-action rules); model-based (internal state); goal-based (considers future outcomes against a goal); utility-based (trade-offs via a utility function); learning agent improves its components from feedback; difficulties: value estimation, exploration vs exploitation, non-stationarity when others learn.

A simple reflex agent maps the current percept to an action with condition-action rules (vacuum: suck if dirty, else move). A model-based reflex agent keeps internal state about the parts of the world it cannot currently see. A goal-based agent uses goal information and predicts what its actions lead to, which brings in search and planning. A utility-based agent scores outcomes with a utility function (an internal version of the performance measure), so it can trade off conflicting goals and handle uncertainty. A learning agent can be any of these, plus learning: modifying each component of the agent to agree better with the available feedback, which improves its overall performance.

Learning a policy is hard because (1) the value of actions is difficult to estimate from noisy, delayed feedback; (2) the agent must balance exploration (trying actions to learn about them) against exploitation (using the best known action); and (3) environments can be non-stationary. In a multi-agent system the other agents are learning too, so from each agent’s view the environment keeps changing and old value estimates go stale.

What is an LLM agent? Explain the thought-action-observation loop and how ReAct implements it, linking each step to a component of the agent.

Key points: acts, observes, reasons and plans through natural language; token completion is multi-task; LLM plus role, memory, tools, planning; loop: reason/plan, act, observe; ReAct (Yao et al., ICLR 2023) prompts interleaved verbal reasoning and actions; Thought = reasoning (CoT), Action = tools, Observation = memory (tool output in context).

An LLM agent is an agent whose reasoning, planning and actions happen in natural language. A language model can play this role because next-token completion is multi-task: the same mechanism answers world-knowledge, history, planning and arithmetic prompts. The model becomes an agent when it is given a role, memory, tools and planning, and placed in a loop with an environment.

The loop has three steps: reason and plan in text, act, observe the result, then repeat. ReAct is a prompting technique that makes a language model generate verbal reasoning and actions, both as text, iteratively as Thought, Action, Observation. The Thought forces multi-step chain-of-thought reasoning; the Action is text that calls an external tool; the Observation inserts the tool’s output into the model’s context, which serves as its memory. The cycle continues until the agent produces a final answer.

Explain how LLM agents handle memory and tools. Distinguish short-term from long-term memory, and list the problems that tool use raises.

Key points: memory = facts, past interactions, context; key to go from LLM to agent; short-term = limited context window, context engineering, trimming or summarising; long-term = external databases or knowledge in parameters; tools = external functions that let agents act; creation, definition, selection, calling, output processing; MCP standardises connection.

Memory lets an agent keep facts, previous interactions and context; without it each step starts from nothing, which is why memory is key to going from an LLM to an agent. Short-term memory is the context window. It is limited, so what enters it must be chosen (context engineering), and long histories are trimmed or summarised. Long-term memory is either external, a database the agent retrieves from, or internal, the knowledge stored in the model’s parameters. Retrieval therefore serves as an agent’s long-term memory, and in the other direction agent-centric information access (Kanoulas et al.) retrieves among expert agents.

Reasoning lets an agent plan; tools let it act. A tool is an external function the model can use, such as search or code execution. Tool use raises five problems: creating and documenting tools so an LLM can use them, defining them so the agent knows they exist, selecting the right tool, calling it (parsing and executing the call), and processing its output back into the LLM. Toolformer showed models can teach themselves tool use; the Model Context Protocol standardises how LLMs connect to tools.

What are reasoning LLMs, and how can reasoning and planning in LLM agents be obtained or improved?

Key points: generate thought tokens before the answer; shift from train-time to test-time compute; prompting (CoT, zero- or few-shot) elicits reasoning in untuned models; search and verify; fine-tuning with RL (DeepSeek-R1); planning = decomposing into sub-tasks; CoT, Least-to-Most, Plan-and-Solve; fine-tuning (SFT, RL) for planning and the ReAct cycle; Reflexion.

A reasoning LLM produces thoughts as tokens before its final answer. This moves effort from train-time compute to test-time compute: more tokens at answer time means more computation on the problem. Reasoning can be elicited by prompting, with chain-of-thought prompting in zero-shot or few-shot form, even in models not tuned for reasoning. It can be improved by search and verify (sample many reasoning traces and reward the best) or by fine-tuning the model’s token probabilities for reasoning, for example with reinforcement learning, as in DeepSeek-R1.

Planning uses reasoning to find the steps that reach a goal: decompose the task into sub-tasks and generate an action sequence. Early methods were prompting techniques (CoT, Least-to-Most, Plan-and-Solve). Models can also be fine-tuned, by supervised fine-tuning or RL, to plan and to run the ReAct cycle better. Reflexion adds verbal reinforcement learning: the agent learns from feedback through reflections written in language.

What risks arise when many LLM agents interact? Use the categories of Hammond et al. and the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.

Key points: miscoordination, conflict, collusion; agents communicated through a software repository service in unexpected ways; agent communication is not inherently problematic but can create risk; models tampered with outputs and logs, abused context compaction, injected code into the evaluator’s container, printed adversarial outputs; explicit about it in their CoT; behaviour depends on how rewards are defined.

Hammond et al. (2025) identify three under-explored risks of LLM-based multi-agent systems: miscoordination, conflict and collusion. The incident shows related risks in practice. Agents used Artifactory in unexpected ways to communicate with each other before the Hugging Face incident; the incident report notes that OpenAI’s models are trained to communicate when given a multi-agent collaboration tool, and that such communication is not inherently problematic but can create risk. The models also tried to deceive their evaluator, to hide that they had obtained an answer flag by cheating: erasing or tampering with outputs and message logs, abusing context compaction, injecting malicious code into the evaluator’s container and printing adversarial outputs, while stating these attempts openly in their chain-of-thought.

The lesson ties back to simple agents: the components that make agents useful (communication, memory, tools) are also routes for deception, and whether agents deceive depends on how their rewards and payoffs are defined, which is rarely trivial.

Using the Prisoner's Dilemma, the Stag Hunt and the vacuum world, explain why simple agents can produce outcomes nobody wants.

Key points: PD: D dominates, (D,D) the only equilibrium, worse for both than (C,C); Stag Hunt: (C,C) and (D,D) both equilibria, C risky; at 50% C, D earns 2.5 vs 2 so C declines; vacuum: two rewards give the same behaviour until Dump exists, then reward 2 dumps and re-sucks; design rewards for the outcome wanted.

In the Prisoner’s Dilemma (C,C = 3,3; C,D = 0,5; D,D = 1,1) defecting pays more whatever the other does (5 > 3, 1 > 0), so rational agents reach (D, D), which both rank below (C, C): a cooperation dilemma. In the Stag Hunt (C,C = 4,4; C,D = 0,3; D,D = 2,2) the best reply matches the partner, so both (C, C) and (D, D) are equilibria; (C, C) is better but risky, a coordination dilemma. In a population with 50% of each type meeting at random, C earns 2 and D 2.5 on average, so if successful strategies spread, cooperators decline.

In the vacuum world, rewarding each clean square per time step and rewarding each unit of dirt sucked produce the same behaviour with Left, Right and Suck. Add Dump and the second reward is maximised by dumping dirt and sucking it again forever. Rewards should describe the outcome wanted in the environment, not the behaviour the designer expects.

L02 Game Theory and Population Dynamics

Exam questions

Describe the hierarchy of game models from one-shot normal-form games to partially observable stochastic games. Give each model's formal definition, say what it adds to the previous one, and how agents' policies change.

Key points: normal-form (I,{Ai​},{Ri​}), no time or state, Ri​ on joint actions, policies are distributions over actions; repeated: same game over time, policies condition on action history ht=(a0,…,at−1); stochastic game (I,S,{Ai​},{Ri​},T,μ) adds states, transitions, initial distribution; POSG adds observation sets Oi​ and functions Oi​:A×S×Oi​→[0,1], policies condition on observation histories; each model contains the previous one, with an example of each.

A normal-form game is a tuple (I,{Ai​},{Ri​}): a finite set of agents I, a finite action set Ai​ for each agent, and reward functions Ri​:A→R on the joint actions A=A1​×⋯×An​. There is no time and no state, only actions and rewards. Each agent follows a policy πi​, a distribution over its actions. Examples: the Prisoner’s Dilemma and Stag Hunt (general-sum), Matching Pennies (zero-sum), a common-reward coordination game.

A repeated normal-form game plays the same game over time steps. Policies become conditioned on the history of joint actions, πi​(ait​∣ht) with ht=(a0,…,at−1), which allows strategies such as Tit-for-Tat and Win-Stay Lose-Shift. The number of steps matters for which strategies do well.

A stochastic game (I,S,{Ai​},{Ri​},T,μ) adds a finite set of states S, a transition function T (the probability of the next state given the current state and joint action) and an initial state distribution μ; rewards can depend on the state. Each state can carry its own game, and actions affect both the immediate reward and the future state. Examples: a three-state game with a matrix per state, the vacuum world (one agent), a foraging grid world with two agents.

A partially observable stochastic game adds, for each agent, a finite observation set Oi​ and an observation function Oi​:A×S×Oi​→[0,1], the probability of each observation given the joint action and resulting state. Agents get incomplete information about the state and others’ actions, so policies condition on their own observation history hit​=(oi0​,…,oit−1​). Examples: autonomous driving, card games with hidden hands, agents in a grid world that see only nearby cells. Each model is a special case of the next: a repeated normal-form game is a stochastic game with one state, and a stochastic game is a POSG where observations reveal the state.

Define a best response and a Nash equilibrium formally. What did Nash prove, and what are the three limitations of the Nash equilibrium as a solution concept?

Key points: BRi​(π−i​)=argmaxπi​​Ui​(⟨πi​,π−i​⟩); NE: ∀i,πi′​: Ui​(⟨πi′​,π−i​⟩)≤Ui​(π), mutual best response; Nash 1950: every finite general-sum normal-form game has an equilibrium, possibly mixed; sub-optimality (PD) and non-uniqueness (SH, possibly infinitely many, different returns); incompleteness (off-equilibrium paths, how equilibria are reached).

A best response of agent i to the other agents’ policies π−i​ is a policy that maximises i‘s expected return given them: BRi​(π−i​)=argmaxπi​​Ui​(⟨πi​,π−i​⟩), where ⟨πi​,π−i​⟩ is the complete joint policy and Ui​ the expected return. A Nash equilibrium is a joint policy π in which every agent’s policy is a best response to the others’: for every agent i and every alternative policy πi′​, Ui​(⟨πi′​,π−i​⟩)≤Ui​(π). No agent can improve its expected return by changing its own policy while the others keep theirs.

Nash (1950) proved that every finite general-sum normal-form game has at least one Nash equilibrium if mixed policies are allowed (by a fixed-point argument). Rock-Paper-Scissors has no pure equilibrium but a mixed one, each action with probability 1/3.

Limitations. (1) Sub-optimality: equilibria need not maximise returns; in the Prisoner’s Dilemma (D, D) is the equilibrium while (C, C) gives both more. (2) Non-uniqueness: there can be several, even infinitely many, equilibria with different returns, as in the Stag Hunt, and the concept does not say which is played. (3) Incompleteness: in sequential games equilibria do not specify actions off the equilibrium path, and the concept does not say how agents reach an equilibrium. The first two motivate refinements such as Pareto optimality, welfare and fairness; the third motivates dynamic approaches such as evolutionary game theory.

In the game below (row player's payoff first), find all pure Nash equilibria, the Pareto-optimal outcomes, and the welfare-optimal and fairness-optimal outcomes. Rows U, D; columns L, R; (U, L) = 5, 1; (U, R) = 0, 0; (D, L) = 1, 1; (D, R) = 3, 3.

Key points: best responses: row U against L, D against R, column L against U, R against D; pure NE (U, L) and (D, R); Pareto optimal (U, L) and (D, R); welfare 6, 0, 2, 6, so both NE are welfare-optimal; fairness 5, 0, 1, 9, so (D, R) is the only fairness-optimal outcome.

Nash. Against L the row player prefers U (5 > 1); against R it prefers D (3 > 0). Against U the column player prefers L (1 > 0); against D it prefers R (3 > 1). Cells where both are best-responding: (U, L) and (D, R). (U, R) and (D, L) are not equilibria: at (U, R) the row player gains by switching to D, at (D, L) the column player gains by switching to R.

Pareto. (D, R) = (3, 3) dominates (D, L) = (1, 1) and (U, R) = (0, 0). (U, L) = (5, 1) and (D, R) = (3, 3) do not dominate each other (the row player prefers the first, the column player the second), so both are Pareto optimal.

Welfare W=U1​+U2​: 6, 0, 2, 6. Both (U, L) and (D, R) are welfare-optimal; the sum cannot separate them. Fairness F=U1​⋅U2​: 5, 0, 1, 9. Only (D, R) is fairness-optimal, because the product prefers the equal split.

Show that Rock-Paper-Scissors (win 1, lose −1, tie 0) has no pure Nash equilibrium, and that both players choosing each action with probability 1/3 is a Nash equilibrium. What kind of game is it?

Key points: zero-sum (payoffs in each cell sum to 0); in every pure cell the loser, or either player at a tie, can switch to the beating action and gain; against uniform play each pure action earns 31​(0−1+1)=0, so every mixed policy is also worth 0; no profitable deviation, so uniform play is a NE; consistent with Nash’s existence result.

It is a zero-sum game: in every cell one player’s gain is the other’s loss. No pure equilibrium: at a tie, either player can switch to the action that beats the other’s and get 1 instead of 0; at a win for one player, the loser can switch to the action that beats the winner’s and get 1 instead of −1. So in every pure cell some player has a profitable deviation.

Mixed equilibrium. Suppose the column player plays R, P, S with probability 1/3 each. The row player’s expected payoff from R is 31​⋅0+31​⋅(−1)+31​⋅1=0, and by symmetry also 0 from P and from S. Any mixed policy averages these, so it also earns 0. No deviation earns more than the uniform policy’s 0, so uniform play is a best response to uniform play, and by symmetry the same holds for the column player. Both best-responding means a Nash equilibrium, which illustrates Nash’s theorem: equilibria always exist once mixed policies are allowed.

Why does evolutionary game theory study populations of agents instead of rational players? Explain the idea of frequency-dependent fitness, state the replicator equation with its terms, and give its three interpretations.

Key points: static solution concepts do not say how equilibria are reached (von Neumann and Morgenstern: theory “thoroughly static”), and real agents use trial and error, incomplete information, imitation; biology plus game theory, Maynard Smith and Price in the 1970s; fitness depends on the frequency of other types, like payoffs on others’ strategies; x˙=x(fC​(x)−fˉ​(x)), C replicates when fitter than average; biology (natural selection), economics (imitation), computer science (RL dynamics, Börgers and Sarin).

Solution concepts such as the Nash equilibrium are static: they say which joint policies are stable but are silent on how agents get there, and they assume rational agents computing best responses. Von Neumann and Morgenstern called their own theory “thoroughly static” and a dynamic theory more complete. Real agents often learn by trial and error, have incomplete information and imitate others, so we ask how the strategies in a population change over time depending on what others do.

Evolutionary game theory combines evolutionary biology and game theory, following Maynard Smith and Price in the 1970s. In natural selection fit types spread, but fitness cannot be measured in isolation: it depends on how frequent the other types are, exactly as a payoff in game theory depends on the others’ strategies.

The replicator equation: x˙=x(fC​(x)−fˉ​(x)), where x is the fraction using strategy C, fC​(x) the average payoff (fitness) of C when a fraction x uses C, and fˉ​(x)=xfC​+(1−x)fD​ the population’s average fitness. C replicates when it is fitter than average, at a rate proportional to its current share. The same equation describes replication and natural selection in biology, social learning by imitation in economics, and reinforcement learning dynamics in computer science (Börgers and Sarin showed that simple reinforcement learning follows it on average).

Derive the two-strategy replicator equation x˙=x(1−x)(fC​−fD​). Apply it to the Stag Hunt (R=4,S=0,T=3,P=2): find the rest points and their stability, and say what happens to a population that starts with 50% C.

Key points: fˉ​=xfC​+(1−x)fD​ gives fC​−fˉ​=(1−x)(fC​−fD​); fC​=4x, fD​=3x+2(1−x), so x˙=x(1−x)(3x−2); rest points 0 (stable), 2/3 (unstable), 1 (stable); at x=1/2, x˙=−1/8, C decreases to 0; the interior point is the mixed NE and a tipping point.

Derivation. fˉ​=xfC​+(1−x)fD​, so fC​−fˉ​=(1−x)fC​−(1−x)fD​=(1−x)(fC​−fD​), and multiplying by x gives x˙=x(1−x)(fC​−fD​). Since x(1−x)>0 for 0<x<1, the sign of fC​−fD​ decides the direction.

Fitness. With random pairing a partner plays C with probability x: fC​=4x+0⋅(1−x)=4x and fD​=3x+2(1−x)=2+x. So fC​−fD​=3x−2 and x˙=x(1−x)(3x−2).

Rest points. x=0, x=1, and x=2/3 where 3x−2=0. For x<2/3, x˙<0; for x>2/3, x˙>0. So the population moves away from 2/3 on both sides: 2/3 is unstable, and 0 and 1 are stable (also g′(0)=S−P=−2<0, g′(1)=T−R=−1<0).

50% C. x˙(1/2)=21​⋅21​⋅(−21​)=−81​<0: C agents earn 2 on average against D agents’ 2.5, so C decreases, and keeps decreasing to x=0, all D. The interior rest point is the mixed Nash equilibrium, but it is a tipping point: populations above two thirds C go to all C, below to all D. Equilibrium selection in the Stag Hunt depends on where the population starts.

Analyse the donation game ( b>c>0) and the Hawk-Dove game ((C,C) = 3,3; (C,D) = 2,8; (D,C) = 8,2; (D,D) = −2,−2) under the replicator dynamics. For each, give the Nash equilibrium, the long-run population, and compare with the Stag Hunt.

Key points: donation: NE (D,D), social optimum (C,C); fC​=xb−c, fD​=xb, x˙=−cx(1−x)<0, all D from any start; Hawk-Dove: symmetric NE mixed with C at 4/9, x˙=x(1−x)(4−9x); 0 and 1 unstable, 4/9 stable, coexistence; mixed equilibrium unstable in the Stag Hunt, stable in Hawk-Dove.

Donation game. Payoffs (C,C) = b−c each, (C,D) = −c, b; (D,C) = b, −c; (D,D) = 0. D earns c more than C against either action, so (D, D) is the unique Nash equilibrium, while (C, C) maximises the sum, 2(b−c)>0. In a population, fC​=x(b−c)+(1−x)(−c)=xb−c and fD​=xb, so x˙=x(1−x)(−c)<0 for all interior x: cooperators decline from any start and the population ends fully D. x=1 is an unstable rest point, since a single defector earns b>b−c.

Hawk-Dove. Against C, D is better (8 > 3); against D, C is better (2 > −2). The symmetric equilibrium is mixed: with the partner playing C with probability q, C earns 2+q and D earns 10q−2, equal at q=4/9. (There are also asymmetric pure equilibria (C, D) and (D, C).) In a population, fC​=3x+2(1−x)=2+x and fD​=8x−2(1−x)=10x−2, so x˙=x(1−x)(4−9x). Rest points 0, 4/9, 1; x˙>0 below 4/9 and <0 above, so 4/9 is stable and the pure states are unstable (g′(0)=S−P=4>0, g′(1)=T−R=5>0). The population converges to coexistence, about 44% C, because each strategy earns more when it is rare.

Comparison. In the Stag Hunt the interior rest point (the mixed equilibrium at 2/3) is unstable and populations go to all C or all D depending on the start. In Hawk-Dove the mixed equilibrium is the stable outcome. In the donation game there is no interior rest point and the Nash prediction (all D) is reached from everywhere.

L03 Intro to Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Exam questions

How does reinforcement learning differ from supervised learning? Describe the components of an RL problem and explain what makes a state Markov.

Key points: RL is closed-loop and sequential, supervised learning open-loop; RL data is not i.i.d. and has rewards instead of labels; agent = policy πθ​(a∣s), environment = MDP {S,A,T,r}, goal = maximise expected (discounted) return; Markov: the state summarises the past as far as the future is concerned; hidden information such as a battery level breaks it.

In supervised learning someone provides a fixed dataset of inputs with correct labels, assumed i.i.d., and the model learns fθ​(x)≈y; the model’s outputs do not change the data it sees, so it is open-loop. RL is sequential decision making: the agent’s actions shape what it sees next. It observes a state, chooses an action, and receives a reward and the next state, so the data is a trajectory produced by its own policy. That data is not i.i.d. (consecutive samples are correlated and depend on the policy), and there are no labels, only a reward saying how good the outcome was.

The agent is its policy πθ​(a∣s), a probability over actions in each state with parameters θ. The environment is a Markov decision process: states S, actions A, transition probabilities P(s′∣s,a) and a reward function R(s,a,s′). The goal is to maximise the expected discounted return E[∑k​γkrt+k​]. Algorithms repeat: run the policy to generate samples, estimate returns or fit a model, improve the policy.

A state is Markov when it is a complete summary of the past as far as the future is concerned: the distribution of the next state given the current state and action does not change when earlier history is added. A robot’s grid position is Markov only if nothing else matters. If the robot has a battery the state does not include, the same cell can lead to different futures depending on how long it has been running, so the position alone is no longer Markov.

Define Vπ and Qπ, write the Bellman equations for a policy, and explain how iterating them leads to value iteration. Why does this approach need a model?

Key points: Vπ and Qπ as expected discounted returns, specific to a policy; Vπ=∑a​πQπ, V∗=maxa​Q∗; Bellman equations as self-consistency conditions, iterated until values stop changing; a greedy policy turns the average into a max (value iteration, a moving target, optimal when it stops changing); needs P and R, often unavailable or intractable.

Vπ(s)=Eπ​[∑t​γtrt​∣s0​=s] is the expected discounted return from s following π; Qπ(s,a) is the same but with action a taken first. Both depend on the policy. They are related by Vπ(s)=∑a​π(a∣s)Qπ(s,a), and for the optimal policy V∗(s)=maxa​Q∗(s,a).

The Bellman equations express self-consistency: Vπ(s)=∑a​π(a∣s)[r(s,a)+γ∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)Vπ(s′)], and similarly Qπ(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)∑a′​π(a′∣s′)Qπ(s′,a′). A state’s value is the step reward plus the discounted expected value of where you land. The values are right when these hold in every state. Starting from any guess and applying them as updates to all states until the values stop changing evaluates the policy.

If the policy is made greedy with respect to the current values, π(s)=argmaxa​[r(s,a)+γ∑s′​PV(s′)], the update becomes V(s)←maxa​[r(s,a)+γ∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)V(s′)]: value iteration. It chases a moving target, since the policy being evaluated improves after every update, and when the values stop changing the greedy policy is optimal. This works by exploiting the Markov property (decisions can be made state by state) instead of searching ∣A∣∣S∣ policies.

The catch is that every update uses P(s′∣s,a) and R. In most problems that model is unknown, or so large that it is intractable (Atari games have astronomically many states); usually there is only a simulator to sample from.

Derive the Q-learning update from the Bellman equation for Q, give its pseudocode, and explain the challenges that learning from samples brings.

Key points: without a model, replace the expectation over next states by one observed transition (s,a,r,s′); greedy target r+γmaxa′​Q(s′,a′); move by learning rate α towards it; full pass against single sample, noisy target; pseudocode with ε-greedy action choice; challenges: exploration, noisy or high-variance updates and credit assignment, data efficiency.

The Bellman update for Q is Q(s,a)←r(s,a)+γ∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)∑a′​π(a′∣s′)Q(s′,a′). Without P and R, the agent can only act and observe a transition (s,a,r,s′). Q-learning replaces the expectation over s′ with that single sample and uses the greedy policy in the target, giving the target r+γmaxa′​Q(s′,a′). Because one sample is noisy, the estimate moves only a fraction α of the way: Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α[r+γmaxa′​Q(s′,a′)−Q(s,a)].

Pseudocode: initialise Q to 0. For each episode, start in s; until terminal, choose a ε-greedily from Q, take it, observe r and s′, set target =r if s′ is terminal and r+γmaxa′​Q(s′,a′) otherwise, update Q(s,a) by α times the TD error, set s←s′. Decay ε and α over episodes; return the greedy policy.

Dynamic programming does a full pass over every state, action and outcome; Q-learning uses one state, one action, one outcome. That brings challenges. Exploration: the agent learns only about states it visits, so it needs an exploration schedule. Noise and credit assignment: single-sample targets give biased, high-variance updates, and delayed rewards have to be traced back to their causes. Data efficiency: samples may be expensive. Value iteration is simple and fast but needs the model; Q-learning needs no prior knowledge but is slower.

Computation: an agent has Q(s,a)=2, takes a, receives r=1 and lands in s′ with maxa′​Q(s′,a′)=4. With α=0.25 and γ=0.5, what is the new Q(s,a)? What would it be if s′ were terminal?

Key points: target =r+γmaxa′​Q(s′,a′)=1+0.5×4=3; TD error =3−2=1; new Q=2+0.25×1=2.25; terminal: target =1, error =−1, new Q=1.75.

The Q-learning update is Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α[r+γmaxa′​Q(s′,a′)−Q(s,a)]. The target is 1+0.5×4=3. The TD error is 3−2=1. The new value is 2+0.25×1=2.25. Equivalently, as a running average: (1−0.25)×2+0.25×3=1.5+0.75=2.25.

If s′ is terminal there is no future value, so the target is just r=1. The TD error is 1−2=−1 and the new value is 2+0.25×(−1)=1.75.

What does the discount factor do? Compute the effective horizon for γ=0.9 and γ=0.99, find the γ with an effective horizon of 50 steps, and use the apple orchard to explain how γ changes the solution. Then explain the learning rate's role.

Key points: γ sets the present value of future rewards, balancing short and long term; effective horizon 1/(1−γ): 10 and 100 steps, γ=0.98 for 50; needed for infinite-horizon tasks, usually high (0.99); orchard: low γ over-harvests, high γ leaves apples to regrow; α weighs new samples against current beliefs (running average); high α fine when deterministic, noisy when stochastic; low α slow; decay.

The discount factor γ∈[0,1) weights a reward k steps ahead by γk, so it sets the present value of future rewards and balances short-term against long-term gains. The effective horizon is 1/(1−γ), because the weights sum to ∑k​γk=1/(1−γ): for γ=0.9 it is 1/0.1=10 steps, for γ=0.99 it is 1/0.01=100 steps. For a horizon of 50, 1/(1−γ)=50 gives γ=1−1/50=0.98. γ is needed mainly for infinite-horizon tasks, where it keeps the sum of rewards finite, and is usually set high (0.99).

γ also changes which solution is found. In an orchard where apples regrow at a rate depending on how many are left, an agent with low γ cares only about rewards soon, so it picks every apple now and the orchard stops producing. With high γ, future harvests count, so it leaves enough apples to regrow and harvests sustainably.

The learning rate α controls how much a new sample is trusted against the current estimate: the update is a running average Q←(1−α)Q+α⋅target. In a deterministic environment a high α is fast and fine, and a low one only slows learning. In a stochastic environment a high α makes the estimate jump with every lucky or unlucky outcome so it never settles, while a low α is smooth and accurate but slow. The usual compromise is to decay α: large early, small later.

Computation: with 5 actions and ε=0.1, give the ε-greedy probability of each action. Compare ε-greedy with Boltzmann exploration, and explain why exploration needs a schedule.

Key points: greedy action 1−0.1+0.1/5=0.92; each other action 0.1/5=0.02 (sum 0.92+4×0.02=1); ε-greedy simple and easy to decay, exploration blind; Boltzmann exp(Q/τ)/∑exp(Q/τ), value-aware, hard to tune; too little exploration sticks to the suboptimal, too much wastes samples, so decay.

With probability 1−ε=0.9 the agent takes the greedy action; with probability 0.1 it picks uniformly among all 5 actions, which can also be the greedy one. So the greedy action has probability 0.9+0.1/5=0.92 and each of the other four 0.1/5=0.02; the total is 0.92+0.08=1.

ε-greedy is simple and easy to decay, but its exploration is blind: a catastrophic action is tried as often as a nearly optimal one. Boltzmann exploration chooses a with probability exp(Q(s,a)/τ)/∑a′​exp(Q(s,a′)/τ), so it is value-aware: better actions are tried more. Its temperature τ is hard to tune, because the right value depends on the scale of the Q-values; low τ is nearly greedy, high τ nearly uniform.

Exploration is needed because an agent that never tries an action never finds out it is better: one that keeps refining the first path it found to a +2 goal never discovers a +5 goal. Too much exploration wastes samples on actions already known to be bad. A decay schedule explores a lot early, when little is known, and exploits more later.

Computation: classify each game as fully cooperative, zero-sum or general-sum, and say what learning has to achieve in each kind: (i) (4,4) (0,0) / (0,0) (2,2); (ii) (1,−1) (−1,1) / (−1,1) (1,−1); (iii) (3,3) (0,5) / (5,0) (1,1).

Key points: rule: equal payoffs in every cell = fully cooperative, payoffs summing to zero in every cell = zero-sum, otherwise general-sum; (i) fully cooperative, (ii) zero-sum (matching pennies), (iii) general-sum (Prisoner’s Dilemma); cooperative needs coordination of tasks, general-sum balancing individual and group welfare (Pareto inefficiency), zero-sum robustness to many opponents.

Compare the two payoffs in each cell. In (i) they are always identical, R1​=R2​, so the game is fully cooperative: both agents want the same thing, and the challenge is coordinating on the better outcome (4,4) over (2,2). In (ii) every cell sums to zero, R1​=−R2​, so it is zero-sum (matching pennies): one agent’s win is the other’s loss, my changes prompt my opponent’s counter-changes, and the aim is a policy robust to many kinds of opponent. In (iii) the payoffs differ and the sums are 6, 5, 5 and 2, so it is neither: general-sum, the Prisoner’s Dilemma. Agents have their own preferences, so besides coordinating they must balance individual and group welfare, and learners struggle with Pareto inefficiency, here mutual defection (1,1), which both agents rank below (3,3).

The payoff structure matters because it defines what a good solution is, what can go wrong and which algorithms make sense.

Define a stochastic game and formulate the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma as one. Why is "maximise your return" no longer an adequate solution concept, and what does MARL optimise for instead?

Key points: multi-agent generalisation of an MDP, N agents acting simultaneously, each with its own reward; tuple (N,S,{Ai},P,{Ri},γ) with transitions and rewards depending on the joint action; IPD: N=2, states CC, CD, DC, DD (last joint action), actions C, D, rewards from the PD matrix; Ji depends on all policies; alternatives: stability (Nash equilibrium), no regret, social welfare, robustness to opponents.

A stochastic game generalises an MDP to N agents that act simultaneously, each with its own reward. It is the tuple (N,S,{Ai},P,{Ri},γ): the set of agents, a shared state space, an action set per agent, a transition function P(s′∣s,a1,…,aN) that depends on the joint action, a reward function Ri(s,a1,…,aN,s′) for each agent, and a discount factor.

The iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma has N=2. The state is the previous round’s joint action, S={CC,CD,DC,DD}, and each agent’s actions are {C,D}. The next state is fixed by the current joint action (play C and D and the next state is CD). Rewards follow the PD matrix: 3 each for mutual cooperation, 5 and 0 when one defects on a cooperator, 1 each for mutual defection. Policies can condition on the state, for example cooperating if the other cooperated last round.

Each agent’s objective is Ji(π1,…,πN)=E[∑t​γtRti​∣π1,…,πN]: its return depends on everyone’s policies, but it controls only its own. “Maximise your return” therefore does not pin down a solution, because my best policy depends on yours and yours on mine. MARL optimises instead for stability (a Nash equilibrium, where no agent gains by changing only its own policy), no regret, social welfare (total reward), or robustness to many kinds of opponent, depending on the setting.

Using matching pennies, explain why convergence in multi-agent learning is not as simple as in an MDP, and give the different notions of convergence.

Key points: in an MDP, converged = the policy stops changing; matching pennies: matcher against mismatcher, zero-sum; any change by one player gives the other a reason for the opposite change, so learning dynamics orbit; equilibrium 0.5/0.5; cycling policies match the equilibrium on average and earn the same average reward; notions: exact policy, average policy over many episodes, average reward.

In an MDP, learning has converged when the policy stops changing, and the optimal policy is then reached. In matching pennies each player picks heads or tails; the row player wins (+1, the other −1) if they match, the column player if they differ, like a goalkeeper and a penalty taker. If the row player leans towards heads, the column player’s best response is tails; then the row player’s best response is tails, then the column player’s is heads, and so on. Any change one makes gives the other a reason to make the opposite change, so the learning dynamics orbit around the equilibrium, where each plays heads with probability 0.5, and the policies never settle.

Yet averaged over time the cycling policies play each action half the time and earn the equilibrium’s average reward (0 each). Whether they have “converged” depends on the notion: the policy matching the equilibrium exactly (not satisfied), the policy matching it on average over many episodes (satisfied), or the average reward matching that of the optimal policy (satisfied). Multi-agent learning therefore has to say which property it wants from a solution.

Explain non-stationarity in MARL using the transition function agent i experiences, and describe its consequences.

Key points: other agents are part of agent i‘s environment; Pi(s′∣s,ai)=∑a−i​[∏j=i​πj(aj∣s)]P(s′∣s,ai,a−i) changes whenever π−i changes; single-agent targets move only as own estimates improve, MARL targets also move as others’ policies change; experience has a shelf life; cycling, broken convergence guarantees, noisy targets with low signal-to-noise ratio.

From agent i‘s point of view the other agents are part of the environment. The probability of reaching s′ after playing ai is Pi(s′∣s,ai)=∑a−i​[∏j=i​πj(aj∣s)]P(s′∣s,ai,a−i): the true, fixed transition function averaged over what the others might do, weighted by their policies. When the others learn, π−i changes, so Pi changes too, and so does agent i‘s expected reward. The environment agent i is learning about is not stationary.

In single-agent RL the learning targets move only because the agent’s own estimates improve. In MARL they also move because the other agents’ policies change, so an agent’s experience has a shelf life: old targets it bootstraps from become outdated. Consequences: cycling, where best responses chase each other as in matching pennies and both agents keep improving without converging; broken guarantees, since convergence proofs for MDP methods such as Q-learning assume a fixed environment; and noisy targets, since bootstrapping from stale estimates gives a low signal-to-noise ratio. In practice it is a moving signal that is hard to track, and it gets worse as more agents’ policies change at once.

What is multi-agent credit assignment? Explain it with the lazy agent in level-based foraging and with the fishing environment, and say why it is hardest in fully cooperative games.

Key points: single-agent RL has temporal credit (which earlier action), MARL adds agent credit (whose action); lazy agent: shared team reward reinforces an idle agent when teammates succeed; disentangling needs counterfactuals and many samples, a hard causal inference problem with low signal-to-noise ratio; worst in fully cooperative games (no individual signal); also in general-sum: fishing, wrong lessons from good and bad outcomes.

Single-agent RL faces temporal credit assignment: deciding which earlier actions led to a reward. With several agents there is a new axis: deciding whose actions led to it. In level-based foraging, three agents collect apples and share a team reward of +1 whenever an apple is collected. If A and B do the work while C wanders in a corner, C still receives +1, so whatever C was doing is reinforced. The lazy agent is rewarded because its teammates succeeded.

Separating each agent’s contribution requires counterfactual reasoning (what would have happened had C acted differently?), which takes many samples and a hard exploration effort. It adds a layer to an already hard causal inference problem, at a very low signal-to-noise ratio.

It is worst in fully cooperative games, because a shared reward carries no individual signal at all. It also arises in general-sum games, where rewards are individual but depend on the others. In a fishing environment with a lake that can be depleted, an agent that fishes aggressively while others hold back catches a lot and learns that aggression is good, though it only paid because others held back. An agent that fishes sustainably while the others hold back too catches little and learns that sustainability is bad, though that shared restraint is what keeps the lake stocked. (If the others were fishing aggressively instead, the small catch would be their doing, and the agent would wrongly blame its own sustainable fishing.) In both cases it credits its own action with an outcome that depended on everyone.

What is the equilibrium selection problem? Why is it called native and inescapable, why do learners tend to reach "safe" equilibria, and how does the number of agents affect this and the other challenges?

Key points: games can have several equilibria, and even perfect learners can converge to a suboptimal one; native to multiple agents and not fixed by better learning; path dependence (history and initial conditions decide), some equilibria exist but are unreachable (side of the road, messaging apps, corrupt government); costly exploration mistakes push learners to safe equilibria (stag hunt); more agents: exponential joint spaces (64N, 5N), more policies chasing each other, harder credit assignment, equilibria harder to escape.

Many games have several equilibria, and which one learners end up in is not determined by the game alone. Even perfect learners, each best-responding correctly, can converge to a suboptimal equilibrium. This is native to multi-agent settings and inescapable: it comes from the interaction, not from estimation error, so better single-agent learning does not remove it. Humans show it constantly. Outcomes are path dependent, shaped by history and initial conditions. Some equilibria exist but cannot be reached: driving on the left or on the right are both equilibria, a country keeps whichever history gave it, and the first driver to switch crashes; in each country people use the messaging app their contacts use; corruption persists where playing along pays as long as others do.

Learners tend to converge to safe equilibria because exploration mistakes are costly. In the stag hunt, a hunter who tries for the stag while the partner collects plants gets nothing, while a plant always pays +1, so both learn that plants are safe and the +5 stag equilibrium stays out of reach. It is a very tough exploration problem with hard-to-predict outcomes.

More agents make everything worse. Joint state and action spaces grow exponentially (in an 8×8 grid with 5 actions, 64N joint states and 5N joint actions). Non-stationarity comes from more policies changing at once, credit has to be split among more agents, and equilibria become harder to escape.

What is independent Q-learning? Give its pseudocode, explain what each agent's Q-values estimate, and use the climbing game to explain why independent learners miscoordinate.

Key points: each agent runs ordinary Q-learning over its own actions and treats the others as part of the environment (MDPti​=MDPt+ki​); pseudocode; QA​(a)≈∑b​πB​(b)R(a,b), the reward averaged over the partner’s actions; climbing game: against a roughly uniform partner c averages best (1.7 against −5.7 and −6.3), the −30 dissuades exploring, stuck at (c,c) = 5 (“minimax”) while the optimum (a,a) = 11 is unreachable; centralized Q over joint actions finds 11.

In independent Q-learning each agent i keeps its own table Qi(s,ai) over its own actions and updates it with the ordinary rule Qi(s,ai)←Qi(s,ai)+α[ri+γmaxb​Qi(s′,b)−Qi(s,ai)]. The other agents’ actions never appear; their behaviour is absorbed into the transitions and rewards agent i experiences, so the MDP it faces changes over time.

Pseudocode: initialise every Qi to 0. Each step, every agent picks its action ε-greedily from its own table; the joint action is executed; the next state and each agent’s reward are observed; each agent updates its own entry with its own target; decay ε over time.

In a one-state game with shared reward R(a,b), agent A’s estimate becomes QA​(a)≈∑b​πB​(b)R(a,b), the reward of a averaged over how often B plays each action. In the climbing game (rows a, b, c: 11, −30, 0 / −30, 7, 6 / 0, 0, 5), (a,a) = 11 is the optimal equilibrium and (b,b) = 7 a worse one. Early on the partner explores roughly uniformly, so QA​(a)≈−6.3, QA​(b)≈−5.7 and QA​(c)≈1.7: c looks best because it never risks −30. Both agents drift to c and get stuck at (c,c) = 5, the action with the best worst case. Action a pays only if the partner also plays a, and trying it otherwise costs −30, so (a,a) is unreachable. A centralized learner with one value per joint action sees 11 directly and finds it. With low, decaying exploration the independent learners sometimes reach (b,b), but the outcome varies between runs.

Why is independent learning still widely used despite its problems? Compare centralized and decentralized learning for 2 agents with 6 actions each, and for 3 agents with 5 actions each.

Key points: centralized explores ∣A∣N joint actions, decentralized ∣A∣×N; 2 agents, 6 actions: 36 against 2 × 6 = 12; 3 agents, 5 actions: 125 against 15; averaging hides coordination (problem) but keeps each agent’s space small (benefit); in level-based foraging IQL reaches the optimum sooner than centralized Q; no guarantees, messy, but scales where central learning is intractable; also IPPO, DDPG, SAC; standard baseline.

A centralized learner treats all agents as one, so it must keep track of and explore every joint action: ∣A∣N of them. Independent learners each handle only their own actions: ∣A∣×N in total. With 2 agents and 6 actions that is one choice among 36 against two choices among 6 (12 values per state). With 3 agents and 5 actions it is 125 joint actions against 15.

The averaging in QA​(a)≈∑b​πB​(b)R(a,b) cuts both ways. It is a problem for coordination, because it hides which joint actions are good, as in the climbing game. It is a benefit for scalability, because each agent explores a small space. In level-based foraging with two agents and two apples, independent Q-learning reached the optimal return sooner than centralized Q-learning, though more noisily, because it explores more efficiently as the joint space grows.

So independent Q-learning is messy and has no convergence guarantees (the environment is non-stationary for each agent), but it is not fundamentally broken, and it scales to large, complex environments where central learning becomes intractable. The same idea applies to other single-agent algorithms (IPPO, DDPG, SAC), and independent learning is a standard baseline across MARL.

L04 Deep RL and Intro to Deep MARL

Exam questions

Mock Q13 (DRL 1): Why does tabular Q-learning fail in complex environments? Select all that apply. (A) A table cannot store values for discrete actions. (B) Many states are visited rarely or never during training. (C) What is learned in one row is not used in other rows. (D) The memory needed grows with the number of state-action pairs. (E) The update rule is undefined when rewards are stochastic.

Key points: B, C and D.

  • (A) Wrong: a table is exactly a store of one value per discrete action in each state.
  • (B) Correct: the number of states explodes, so with a fixed budget many rows are rarely or never updated.
  • (C) Correct: no generalisation; each value is updated in isolation.
  • (D) Correct: the table grows with the number of state-action pairs.
  • (E) Wrong: with stochastic rewards the update is a running average and remains well defined.

Mock Q14 (DRL 2): What does the replay buffer of DQN contribute? Select all that apply. (A) It stores earlier copies of the network weights. (B) It turns DQN into an on-policy method. (C) It reduces the correlation between the samples in a minibatch. (D) It removes the need for a target network. (E) It allows each transition to be used for several updates.

Key points: C and E.

  • (A) Wrong: that is the target network; the buffer stores transitions (s,a,r,s′).
  • (B) Wrong: replaying old transitions is only possible because DQN is off-policy.
  • (C) Correct: uniform sampling mixes transitions from many episodes, breaking the correlation of consecutive steps.
  • (D) Wrong: the buffer addresses correlated data, the target network addresses moving targets; DQN uses both.
  • (E) Correct: a stored transition can be sampled many times, which re-uses experience.

Mock Q15 (DRL 3): You add a random binary input that does not affect the game to the state of a Q-table. What is the effect? Select one answer. (a) The rows double, and values are not shared between rows that differ in this input. (b) The rows stay the same, because the table learns to ignore the input. (c) The rows double, but each update also copies the value to the matching row. (d) The rows stay the same, but the optimal policy of the game changes.

Key points: (a).

  • (a) Correct: each state now comes in two versions, and a table has no mechanism to share values between rows.
  • (b) Wrong: a table cannot ignore an input; every distinct input is its own row.
  • (c) Wrong: a table update changes exactly one entry.
  • (d) Wrong: the input does not affect the game, so the optimal policy stays the same, and the table does grow.

Mock Q16 (DRL 4): What are the input and output of a standard DQN? Select one answer. (a) Input: the state. Output: a probability for each discrete action. (b) Input: the state. Output: one Q-value for each discrete action. (c) Input: the state and an action. Output: a probability for that action. (d) Input: an action. Output: the value of each possible next state.

Key points: (b).

  • (a) Wrong: probabilities per action are the output of a policy network.
  • (b) Correct: the state goes in and one output per discrete action gives Q(s,a1​;θ),…,Q(s,a∣A∣​;θ), so one pass gives all values.
  • (c) Wrong: DQN outputs values, and takes no action as input.
  • (d) Wrong: DQN does not predict next states.

Mock Q17 (DRL 5): Which statements about DQN are correct? Select all that apply. (A) It directly learns a network that outputs action probabilities. (B) No gradient flows through the target y during an update. (C) It usually collects data with an ε-greedy policy. (D) It is an off-policy method. (E) It handles continuous actions without any changes.

Key points: B, C and D.

  • (A) Wrong: that describes policy gradient methods; DQN learns Q-values.
  • (B) Correct: the target is computed with the target network and treated as a constant; only the estimate Q(s,a;θ) is differentiated.
  • (C) Correct: actions are chosen ε-greedily from the current Q-network.
  • (D) Correct: the max in its target learns the greedy policy’s values from data collected by ε-greedy and older policies in the buffer.
  • (E) Wrong: it needs one output per discrete action and a max over actions.

Mock Q18 (DRL 6): In DQN, what is the target y when the next state s' is terminal? Select one answer. (a) y = r (b) y = 0 (c) y = r + γ max_a' Q(s', a'; θ⁻) (d) y = max_a' Q(s', a'; θ⁻)

Key points: (a).

  • (a) Correct: after a terminal state no future reward follows, so the target is just the last reward.
  • (b) Wrong: that drops the reward that was actually received.
  • (c) Wrong: that is the non-terminal target; it would add value that cannot be collected.
  • (d) Wrong: it ignores the reward and still bootstraps from the terminal state.

Mock Q19 (DRL 7): In A2C, the estimate Adv(s, a) = r + γ V(s') − V(s) is positive. What does the actor update do? Select one answer. (a) It makes action a more likely, because a did better than expected. (b) It makes action a less likely, because the critic was too pessimistic. (c) It sets the probability of action a to 1 for this state. (d) It leaves the policy unchanged, and only the critic is updated.

Key points: (a).

  • (a) Correct: the actor loss −Advlogπ(a∣s;ϕ) with positive Adv is minimised by raising π(a∣s): the outcome beat the critic’s expectation V(s).
  • (b) Wrong: a positive advantage increases the probability.
  • (c) Wrong: a gradient step moves the probability a little.
  • (d) Wrong: actor and critic are both updated every step.

Mock Q20 (DRL 8): Which quantity does REINFORCE use to estimate the policy gradient at time t? G_t is the Monte Carlo return. Select one answer. (a) G_t ∇_φ max_a Q(s_t, a; φ) (b) π(a_t | s_t; φ) ∇_φ G_t (c) G_t ∇_φ log π(a_t | s_t; φ) (d) ∇_φ (G_t − π(a_t | s_t; φ))²

Key points: (c).

  • (a) Wrong: REINFORCE has no Q-network.
  • (b) Wrong: the return is a sampled number and has no gradient with respect to ϕ.
  • (c) Correct: the policy gradient theorem with Qπ(st​,at​) replaced by the return Gt​.
  • (d) Wrong: that is a regression loss of a probability onto a return, which is meaningless.

Mock Q21 (DRL 9, open, 10 points): Tabular Q-learners play the Coin Game, whose table has 1,458 rows. Each of k random lamps doubles the number of rows (as lamps can be on or off). Training plays 300 updates, each with 32 parallel games of 16 steps, and every step gives one decision per agent. Coins per episode are 14.5 with no lamps and 4.9 with 8 lamps, while random agents collect 3.7. (a) Compute the number of rows N for k = 0 and k = 8, and the budget B of decisions per agent. (3 points) (b) Use these numbers to explain the drop in performance. Why can't agents with tabular learning discover that the lamps do not matter? (3 points) (c) Explain how a neural network avoids this problem. Name one new challenge it introduces. (4 points)

Key points: N=1,458 for k=0 and 1,458⋅28 for k=8, B=300⋅32⋅16; with 8 lamps most rows are never visited and the rest only a few times, unvisited rows hold zeros so the agent acts at random, rows grow while the budget stays; rows differing in one lamp share nothing, so each lesson must be relearned for every lamp pattern; a network computes values or a policy from the observation with shared weights, so what it learns about the coin’s position applies to all lamp patterns and the lamps can get little weight; new challenges: instability from moving targets or correlated data, possible divergence, no general convergence guarantee, more computation.

(a) Without lamps N=1,458. With 8 lamps N=1,458⋅28=373,248. Each agent makes one decision per step, so B=300⋅32⋅16=153,600 decisions.

(b) Without lamps the budget gives about 153,600/1,458≈105 decisions per row, enough to learn useful values. With 8 lamps it is about 153,600/373,248≈0.4 per row: most rows are never visited, and the others only a few times. An unvisited row still holds its initial zeros, so the agent acts at random there, and rows visited once or twice have barely trained values. The number of rows grows by 2k while the budget stays the same, so the probability of visiting each state becomes too low, and performance falls from 14.5 coins to 4.9, close to the 3.7 of random agents. The table cannot discover that the lamps do not matter, because two rows that differ in one lamp share nothing: whatever is learned in one row is not used in the other, so each lesson must be learned again for each of the other lamp patterns.

(c) A neural network computes values or a policy as a function of the observation, with weights shared by all inputs. What it learns about the coin’s position applies to all lamp patterns, and since the lamps carry no information about the return, it can learn to give them little weight. It generalises across the states the table kept apart. New challenges: instability from moving targets (the targets depend on the weights being trained) or from correlated data, possible divergence, no general convergence guarantee, and more computation per decision.

Mock Q22 (DMARL 1): Which of these can reduce the problem of outdated experience in IDQN? Select all that apply. (A) Removing the target network (B) Storing importance sampling weights with the action probabilities of all agents (C) Using a larger replay buffer (D) Using a higher discount factor (E) Using a smaller replay buffer

Key points: B and E.

  • (A) Wrong: the target network addresses moving targets; removing it destabilises learning and leaves the stale data in place.
  • (B) Correct: with the agents’ action probabilities stored, a replayed transition can be reweighted by how likely the others are to act that way now.
  • (C) Wrong: a larger buffer keeps older experience from the others’ older policies, which makes the problem worse.
  • (D) Wrong: the discount factor sets how far ahead the agent looks and has nothing to do with the age of the data.
  • (E) Correct: a smaller buffer holds only recent transitions, generated by policies close to the others’ current ones.

Mock Q23 (DMARL 2): Autonomous cars cannot exchange all sensor data while driving, but a simulator can provide all data during training. Which mode fits best? Select one answer. (a) Centralised training and execution (b) Decentralised training and execution (c) Centralised training with decentralised execution (d) Decentralised training with centralised execution

Key points: (c).

  • (a) Wrong: centralised execution would need the sensor exchange that is impossible while driving.
  • (b) Wrong: it would ignore the full information the simulator offers during training.
  • (c) Correct: training can use the simulator’s shared information, and each car then acts on its own sensors.
  • (d) Wrong: execution is exactly the phase that cannot be centralised here, and it is not one of the three standard modes.

Mock Q26 (DMARL 5): Why can independent REINFORCE adapt faster to other learning agents than IDQN? Select one answer. (a) It learns from recent experience, generated by the current policies of the other agents. (b) It reads the current policy parameters of the other agents during training. (c) It reuses old experience, which covers more policies of the other agents. (d) It uses a centralised critic that is conditioned on the joint action of all agents.

Key points: (a).

  • (a) Correct: REINFORCE is on-policy: each update uses the latest episodes and discards them, while IDQN’s buffer replays experience from the others’ old policies.
  • (b) Wrong: independent learners have no access to the others’ parameters.
  • (c) Wrong: that is IDQN’s replay, the source of the problem.
  • (d) Wrong: a centralised critic belongs to CTDE; independent REINFORCE has no critic at all.

Explain the moving target problem and the problem of correlated experience in deep Q-learning, and how DQN solves each. Give DQN's pseudocode and explain why it can use a replay buffer.

Key points: targets computed with the trained θ, every update changes many values and hence the targets (unlike one table entry); consecutive transitions are not i.i.d., leading to overfitting to recent data and catastrophic forgetting; target network θˉ updated less often; replay buffer with uniform minibatches (also re-use and stable gradients); off-policy because the max target is independent of the behaviour policy.

In deep Q-learning the network is trained to minimise (yt−Q(st,at;θ))2 with target yt=rt+γmaxa′​Q(st+1,a′;θ). Because the target uses the same parameters, and a network generalises, every gradient step changes the values of many states, including those the targets come from. In a table one entry changes per update; here the targets move after every step, which makes learning unstable. Second, transitions arrive in sequence, so consecutive samples are highly correlated and cover a small part of the state space. Gradient descent on such data overfits to recent experience and forgets what was learned elsewhere (catastrophic forgetting).

DQN keeps a target network with parameters θˉ, used only to compute targets r+γmaxa′​Q(s′,a′;θˉ) and copied from θ at set intervals, so targets stay fixed in between. It also stores every transition in a replay buffer and trains on minibatches sampled uniformly from it, which decorrelates the samples, lets each transition be used several times, and averages gradients over a batch.

Pseudocode: initialise θ, set θˉ=θ, empty buffer. Each step: choose at ε-greedily from Q(st,⋅;θ), act, observe rt and st+1, store the transition, sample B transitions, set yk=rk if sk+1 is terminal and rk+γmaxa′​Q(sk+1,a′;θˉ) otherwise, minimise B1​∑k​(yk−Q(sk,ak;θ))2, and at set intervals copy θˉ←θ.

The buffer contains actions chosen by older policies. That is allowed because Q-learning is off-policy: the max in its target estimates the greedy policy’s values whatever policy produced the data.

Derive the motivation for policy gradient methods, state the policy gradient theorem, and explain REINFORCE, including its main weakness and the fix.

Key points: ε-greedy policies over discrete actions cannot express arbitrary or continuous policies; softmax policy network; J(ϕ)=∑s​dπ(s)Vπ(s) and ∇dπ needs the model; theorem ∇J∝E[Qπ∇logπ] without ∇d; REINFORCE uses the Monte Carlo return; unbiased but high variance; baseline b(s) keeps it unbiased and reduces variance.

A value-based agent derives its policy from Q-values, usually ε-greedily, so it can only express “one favourite action plus uniform noise” and needs one output per discrete action. It cannot represent a policy like (0.4, 0.1, 0.5), mixed strategies needed in games such as matching pennies, or continuous actions. A policy network outputs preferences, turned into probabilities by a softmax, so any distribution is reachable.

The objective is J(ϕ)=∑s​dπϕ​(s)Vπϕ​(s). Differentiating the visitation probabilities is hard: changing ϕ changes the action probabilities at every step, early actions change later states, and the exact effect needs the transition model. The policy gradient theorem avoids it: ∇ϕ​J(ϕ)∝Es,a∼π​[Qπ(s,a)∇ϕ​logπ(a∣s;ϕ)]. It raises the probability of each action in proportion to its value, and it can be estimated from samples. Qπ still has to be estimated.

REINFORCE estimates it with the Monte Carlo return. It plays an episode with the current policy, then minimises −T1​∑t​Gt​logπ(at∣st;ϕ) with Gt​=∑τ≥t​γτ−trτ. It is simple, needs no critic, and its gradient estimate is unbiased. Its weakness is high variance: trajectories from the same state can give very different returns, so gradients are noisy and training is unstable and slow; it also has to wait for the end of each episode. The fix is a baseline: use Gt​−b(st). Since ∑a​π∇logπ=0, a state-dependent baseline leaves the expected gradient unchanged while reducing its variance. Using a learned V(s) as the baseline leads to actor-critic methods.

Explain how A2C and PPO improve on REINFORCE. Define the advantage, give the A2C actor and critic losses, and explain the PPO clipped objective.

Key points: actor and critic; advantage Q−V estimated by r+γV(s′)−V(s); actor loss −Advlogπ, critic loss (y−V)2; single-step updates, lower variance, bias from bootstrapping; PPO: a single step can shift the policy too far; ratio ρ=πϕ​/πold​, clip to [1−ϵ,1+ϵ], pessimistic min; several passes over a batch, still on-policy.

A2C learns a policy (the actor) and a state-value estimate (the critic). It replaces the return by the advantage Advπ(s,a)=Qπ(s,a)−Vπ(s), how much better a is than following the policy, estimated in one step as rt+γV(st+1)−V(st) (just rt−V(st) at a terminal step). The actor minimises −Adv(st,at)logπ(at∣st;ϕ), raising the probability of actions that did better than expected and lowering the others; the critic minimises (yt−V(st;θ))2 with yt=rt+γV(st+1;θ), like value-based regression. It updates after every step and has lower variance than REINFORCE, at the price of bias, since the critic’s bootstrapped estimates may be wrong.

Policy gradient steps can still change the policy a lot in one update, a source of instability. PPO limits the change. With ρ=π(a∣s;ϕ)/π(a∣s;ϕold​), the ratio of new to old probability, it minimises −min(ρAdv,clip(ρ,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)Adv). Once a good action’s ratio exceeds 1+ϵ, or a bad action’s falls below 1−ϵ, the clipped term is constant and there is no gradient to move it further. This keeps updates stable and lets PPO run several optimisation passes over each batch of rollouts. It is more complex than REINFORCE, remains generally on-policy, and the clip is no strict guarantee against harmful changes.

Describe the three training and execution modes of multi-agent deep RL, and explain how IDQN and independent policy gradient methods differ in their main weakness.

Key points: centralised uses others’ information, decentralised only the own history; CTCE: one policy over the joint action space, joint reward, does not scale, agents may be distributed; DTDE: independent learning, non-stationarity, poor coordination, unstable; CTDE: shared information or centralised critic in training, local observations in execution; IDQN’s buffer holds experience from others’ old policies (smaller buffers, importance weights); independent policy gradients learn from fresh on-policy data but have amplified variance; IA2C’s critic does not solve credit assignment; IPPO’s clip is per agent.

Training an agent is centralised when it uses information about the other agents (their observations, actions, policies or a global state), decentralised when it conditions only on the agent’s own history; the same distinction applies to execution. Centralised training and execution (CTCE) trains one policy over the joint action space, as if one agent controlled all; it needs a joint reward, does not scale because the joint action space grows exponentially, and is impossible when agents are distributed by design. Decentralised training and execution (DTDE) is independent learning: each agent has only its own model and observations; it uses nothing about the others, faces non-stationarity, coordinates poorly and learns unstably. Centralised training with decentralised execution (CTDE) uses shared information or a centralised critic during training and lets each agent act on its local observations at execution, for example cars trained in a simulator that cannot share sensor data on the road.

In IDQN each agent trains its own DQN with its own replay buffer. The buffer stores transitions produced while the others used older policies; once they change, those transitions describe a different environment, and the agent keeps learning from them. Remedies: a smaller buffer, or storing the agents’ action probabilities and reweighting replayed transitions by importance sampling. Independent policy gradient methods are on-policy, so each update uses experience generated by the others’ current policies and nothing goes stale; they adapt faster. Their weakness is that independent learning amplifies existing instability: Monte Carlo returns in independent REINFORCE vary even more as the others change, IA2C’s critic must track a moving environment and, with a shared team reward, does not solve credit assignment, and IPPO’s clip bounds only each agent’s own change, so the joint policy can still shift a lot.
