L05 Deep MARL, Part II

Exam questions

Mock exam Q23 (DMARL 2, 2 points, select one): Autonomous cars cannot exchange all sensor data while driving, but a simulator can provide all data during training. Which mode fits best? (a) Centralised training and execution (b) Decentralised training and execution (c) Centralised training with decentralised execution (d) Decentralised training with centralised execution

Key points: (c) centralised training with decentralised execution.

The simulator makes all data available during training, so training can be centralised; the cars cannot exchange all their data while driving, so each must act on its own information at execution. (a) needs full data exchange while driving, (b) wastes the simulator’s data, and (d) is backwards.

Mock exam Q24 (DMARL 3, 2 points, select all that apply): Which statements about parameter sharing are correct? (A) It requires agents to exchange their observations during execution. (B) It works best when the optimal policies of the agents differ. (C) It constrains all agents to the same policy. (D) The number of parameters stays constant as the number of agents grows. (E) The shared parameters are updated with the experience of all agents.

Key points: C, D and E.

C: all agents use one set of parameter values, so one policy. D: there is one network however many agents there are. E: every agent’s experience trains the shared network. A is false: each agent runs its own copy of the network on its own observations. B is false: it suits strongly homogeneous agents, whose optimal policies are identical.

Mock exam Q25 (DMARL 4, 2 points, select one): What does a deep agent model of agent i learn to do? (a) Copy the true parameters of agent j at every step of execution (b) Split the common reward into one utility for each agent (c) Predict the actions of agent j from the observation history of agent i (d) Replace the value function of agent i with a smaller network

Key points: (c).

The model π^ji​(aj​∣hi​;ϕji​) takes agent i‘s observation history as input, outputs a distribution over agent j‘s actions, and is trained on j‘s observed actions with the loss −logπ^ji​(ajt​∣hit​). (a) agent i cannot see j‘s parameters; (b) is value decomposition; (d) describes nothing in agent modelling.

Mock exam Q27 (DMARL 6, 2 points, select one): Why can experience sharing be preferred over parameter sharing? (a) It needs less computation per step, as batches become smaller. (b) Agents keep their own networks, so their learned policies can differ. (c) It needs fewer network parameters as the number of agents grows. (d) It needs no correction when applied to on-policy algorithms.

Key points: (b).

Experience sharing only pools the replay data; each agent still trains its own network, so it works for weakly homogeneous agents whose optimal policies differ. (a) and (c) are wrong: it is the more expensive option, with n networks to train. (d) is wrong: on-policy learning from other agents’ trajectories needs a correction such as importance sampling.

Mock exam Q28 (DMARL 7, 2 points, select one): In Policy Space Response Oracles (PSRO), what is the meta-game? (a) A stochastic game whose states are the observation histories of the agents (b) A normal-form game whose actions are the policies in the current populations (c) A common-reward game whose value function is decomposed into utilities (d) A search tree whose nodes are expanded by Monte Carlo tree search

Key points: (b).

PSRO keeps a population of policies per agent. The meta-game is the normal-form game in which each agent “chooses” one of its policies and the payoffs are the expected returns of those policies against each other, estimated by simulation. Solving it gives a distribution over each population, against which a new best-response policy is trained. (c) describes value decomposition and (d) MCTS.

Mock exam Q29 (DMARL 8, open, 10 points): In environment A, two agents must reach the same landmark. In environment B, two agents must reach two different landmarks. In both, the agents have the same actions and observations, and swapping their policies does not change the return. (a) Define weakly and strongly homogeneous agents. Classify the agents in A and in B. (3 points) (b) Give two benefits of parameter sharing. (3 points) (c) Which environment (A or B) can use parameter sharing without observing agent indices? Explain. (2 point) (d) Which alternative suits the other environment, to still use some agent homogeneity to improve learning efficiency? (2 points)

Key points: weakly homogeneous = permuting policies does not change the returns, strongly = the optimal joint policy consists of identical policies; A strongly, B weakly homogeneous; parameters stay constant as agents are added, and shared parameters learn from all agents’ more diverse experience (sample efficiency); A, since its optimal policies are identical, while identical policies in B could not reliably send the agents to different landmarks; experience sharing.

(a) Agents are weakly homogeneous when permuting the policies between agents does not change the returns. They are strongly homogeneous when the optimal joint policy consists of identical policies. In both environments swapping policies leaves the return unchanged, so both are at least weakly homogeneous. In A the best joint policy is for both agents to go to the same landmark, an identical policy for each, so A is strongly homogeneous. In B the agents must split between two landmarks, so their optimal policies differ: B is weakly homogeneous.

(b) With parameter sharing the number of parameters stays constant as agents are added, because all agents use one network. And the shared parameters learn from the more diverse experience of all agents, which improves sample efficiency.

(c) A. Its optimal policies are identical, so one shared policy is exactly what is needed. In B identical policies with the same observations could not reliably send the agents to different landmarks; the shared network would need the agent index to tell the agents apart.

(d) Experience sharing, in which the agents keep their own networks but learn from each other’s trajectories. Weak homogeneity makes the other agent’s experience relevant, and separate networks let the two agents learn different policies.

Describe the three training and execution modes in MARL, with the advantages and disadvantages of each.

Key points: centralised = uses others’ shared information, decentralised = own experience only; CTCE: coordination and help with partial observability, but exponential joint action space and impossible for distributed agents; DTDE: scalable and works without communication, but non-stationary, suboptimal equilibria, cannot attribute changes to other agents; CTDE: shared information only in training, no central controller at execution, accounts for interactions, but training can be a bottleneck and local information may not suffice.

Training is optimising the policy and exploring; execution is selecting actions. A phase is centralised when agent i uses centrally shared information about the others (joint history, observations, global state, joint policy), decentralised when it relies only on its own experience.

Centralised training and execution uses shared information throughout: observation histories, policies, value functions. It improves coordination, and in partially observable stochastic games the pooled observations remove much of the partial information. But the joint action space grows exponentially with the number of agents, and agents may be distributed entities by design.

Decentralised training and execution uses no shared information: independent learning or agent modelling. It scales and works for distributed agents that cannot communicate, but training is affected by non-stationarity, agents can select suboptimal equilibria, and an agent cannot identify which changes are due to other agents.

Centralised training with decentralised execution uses shared information only during training, as in an actor-critic with a centralised critic and decentralised actors. Execution needs no central controller, which suits distributed settings with limited runtime communication, and training can account for the interactions between agents. But centralised training can still be a bottleneck, and coordination is hard when local information is not sufficient during execution.

State the multi-agent policy gradient theorem and explain how it leads to a centralised actor-critic. Describe centralised A2C and explain why a CTDE version of REINFORCE is uncommon.

Key points: ∇ϕi​​J∝E[Qiπ​(h^,⟨ai​,a−i​⟩)∇ϕi​​logπi​(ai​∣hi​;ϕi​)]; evaluation on joint history and joint action, policy on own history; actor π(⋅∣hi​;ϕi​) decentralised, critic V(hi​,z;θi​) centralised and training-only; advantage ri​+γV(hi′​,z′)−V(hi​,z) in the actor loss, squared TD error for the critic; REINFORCE has no critic, so nothing can be centralised.

The single-agent theorem weights ∇ϕ​logπ(a∣s) by Qπ(s,a), so valuable actions become more likely. With several agents the value of agent i‘s action depends on what the others do, so the theorem becomes ∇ϕi​​J(ϕi​)∝Eh^,ai​∼πi​,a−i​∼π−i​​[Qiπ​(h^,⟨ai​,a−i​⟩)∇ϕi​​logπi​(ai​∣hi​;ϕi​)]. Actions are evaluated on the full history and the joint action, while the policy conditions only on agent i‘s own history.

That split is CTDE. The evaluation is only needed to compute gradients during training, so it can use centralised information; the policy is used at execution, so it stays decentralised. In the centralised actor-critic, each agent has an actor π(⋅∣hi​;ϕi​) and a critic V(hi​,z;θi​) whose input adds centralised information z, such as the joint history or global state.

Centralised A2C runs K parallel environments. Each step, every agent samples its action from its actor, the environments return rewards, observations and the next z. For each agent the advantage is ri​+γV(hi′​,z′;θi​)−V(hi​,z;θi​) (just ri​−V at a terminal state); the actor’s loss is minus the advantage-weighted log-probability of its actions, averaged over environments; the critic regresses on the target ri​+γV(hi′​,z′) with a squared loss.

REINFORCE has no critic: it weights the gradient by sampled Monte Carlo returns. Its only learned component is the policy, which must stay decentralised for execution, so there is no training-only part into which centralised information could go.

What problem does value decomposition solve? Define the IGM property, give its two implications, and check it for the decomposition Q1​(A)=0.88, Q1​(B)=4.88, Q2​(A)=0.12, Q2​(B)=4.12 of the common-reward game (A,A) = 1, (A,B) = (B,A) = 5, (B,B) = 9.

Key points: centralised values handle non-stationarity, coordination and partial observability, but in common-reward games credit assignment remains and execution must be decentralised; learn per-agent utilities Q(hi​,ai​;θi​); IGM: argmax of the joint value = tuple of individual argmaxes; implications: greedy decentralised execution, and cheap computation of the greedy joint action; the sums reproduce 1, 5, 5, 9 and both agents choose B, giving the optimal (B, B).

A centralised action-value function Q(h,z,a) conditions on everyone’s information and the joint action. That deals with non-stationarity, coordination and partial observability, but in cooperative, common-reward games it is still hard to learn the team’s best joint policy from one shared reward, because nothing says which agent’s action mattered (credit assignment), and agents still have to select actions on their own at execution. Value decomposition learns one utility Q(hi​,ai​;θi​) per agent, from its own history and action, such that greedy individual actions give the optimal joint action.

The IGM property: argmaxa1​,…,an​​Q(s,a1​,…,an​)=(argmaxa1​​Q1​(o1​,a1​),…,argmaxan​​Qn​(on​,an​)). The joint action that maximises the joint value is the set of individually maximising actions. Implications: each agent can act greedily on its own utility for decentralised execution; and the greedy joint action, needed in every Q-learning target, is found by n small maximisations instead of one over the exponentially large joint action space.

Check: 0.88+0.12=1, 0.88+4.12=5, 4.88+0.12=5, 4.88+4.12=9, so the sum reproduces every reward. Agent 1 prefers B (4.88 > 0.88), agent 2 prefers B (4.12 > 0.12), and (B, B) = 9 is the maximum of the joint table, so IGM holds.

Derive the linear value decomposition behind VDN, give the VDN algorithm, and explain how QMIX generalises it. What can neither represent?

Key points: assume r=∑i​rˉi​; linearity of expectation gives Q(h,z,a)=∑i​Q(hi​,ai​;θi​); VDN: greedy local actions, shared buffer, target r+γ∑i​maxQ(hi′​,ai′​;θˉi​), loss on y−∑i​Qi​; additivity fails when success needs specific combinations (matching); QMIX: monotonic fmix​ with ∂Q/∂Qi​>0, weights from a hypernetwork on z, VDN is the special case; monotonic mixes still cannot represent best actions that flip with the other agent’s action (QTRAN goes further).

If the shared reward is a sum of individual terms rt=rˉ1t​+⋯+rˉnt​, the joint value is the expected discounted sum of ∑i​rˉi​. Swapping the sums by linearity of expectation turns it into a sum of n expectations, each the discounted return of one agent’s term, and approximating each by a utility of that agent’s history and action gives Q(h,z,a;θ)=∑i​Q(hi​,ai​;θi​).

VDN learns this. Each agent picks its action ε-greedily from its own utility. Transitions with the shared reward go into a shared replay buffer. For a mini-batch, the target is r at terminal states and otherwise r+γ∑i​maxai′​​Q(hi′​,ai′​;θˉi​) with target networks; the loss is (y−∑i​Q(hi​,ai​;θi​))2, minimised jointly over all utilities, and target networks are refreshed at intervals. The sum satisfies IGM, and the network decides how to split credit.

The additive assumption is restrictive: when two agents must choose matching actions, the value of an action depends on the partner’s action, and no sum of individual values captures that.

QMIX only requires monotonicity: Q(h,z,a)=fmix​(Q(h1​,a1​),…,Q(hn​,an​);θmix​) with ∂Q/∂Qi​>0 for every agent. Raising a utility never lowers the joint value, so IGM still holds. The mixing parameters come from a hypernetwork fhyper​(z;θhyper​) fed with centralised information, and both the target and the estimate pass the utilities through fmix​. With the sum as mixing function it reduces to VDN. A monotonic mix still cannot represent games where one agent’s best action flips depending on the other’s choice, such as the matching task; methods like QTRAN go beyond it.

Explain agent modelling in deep joint-action learning: what the agent model is, how it is trained and how it is used to select actions. Then explain how LOLA goes further.

Key points: goal: explicitly model the others’ policies to condition on them and adapt to changes; π^ji​(aj​∣hi​;ϕji​), input i‘s observation history, output distribution over j‘s actions; loss −logπ^ji​(ajt​∣hit​); joint-action value Q(hi​,⟨ai​,a−i​⟩) averaged with the models gives AV(hi​,ai​), used for greedy choice and targets; LOLA anticipates the opponent’s gradient step θj​+β∇θj​​Jj​ and differentiates through it.

Independent learners and centralised critics infer the other agents’ behaviour only implicitly from training data. Agent modelling models the others’ policies explicitly, so an agent can condition its action selection on them and adapt when they change.

In deep joint-action learning, agent i keeps one model π^ji​ per other agent j, a network with parameters ϕji​ whose input is agent i‘s observation history and whose output is a probability distribution over j‘s actions. It is trained by minimising −logπ^ji​(ajt​∣hit​;ϕji​), the negative log-likelihood of the actions j was actually seen taking.

Agent i also learns a value over joint actions Q(hi​,⟨ai​,a−i​⟩;θi​), trained like DQN on the observed joint actions. To choose its own action it averages that value over the models’ predictions: AV(hi​,ai​)=∑a−i​​Q(hi​,⟨ai​,a−i​⟩)∏j=i​π^ji​(aj​∣hi​). It acts ε-greedily on AV, and the Q-learning target is ri​+γmaxai′​​AV(hi′​,ai′​;θˉi​).

LOLA uses the fact that the others are learning. A naive learner updates θi​←θi​+α∇θi​​Ji​(θi​,θj​), treating the opponent as fixed. LOLA anticipates the opponent’s step θjt+1​(θi​)=θj​+β∇θj​​Jj​(θi​,θj​) and updates with ∇θi​​Ji​(θi​,θjt+1​(θi​)). Because the opponent’s next parameters depend on θi​, the gradient gains a shaping term: agent i chooses its update partly for how it steers the opponent’s learning.

Why are large two-player zero-sum board games hard for RL, and how do MCTS and self-play (AlphaZero) address this? State the conditions self-play needs.

Key points: two agents, fully observable, turn-taking (chess, shogi, backgammon, Go); sparse reward, large branching factor, long horizon, so efficient game-tree exploration is needed; MCTS: selection, expansion, backpropagation, N←N+1, Q←Q+(G−Q)/N, ε-greedy or UCB; self-play: one policy chooses actions for both agents; needs symmetric roles and egocentric observations; AlphaZero: network-guided MCTS plus self-play.

These games give a reward only at the end (win or lose), have many legal moves per position and last many moves, so random exploration almost never reaches informative outcomes and the tree is far too big to enumerate.

Monte Carlo tree search builds a partial tree from the current position by repeated simulations. In selection it walks down the tree, choosing actions ε-greedily or by UCB on the current statistics; in expansion it adds the first new state reached as a leaf; in backpropagation it sends the simulation’s outcome back up the path, updating N(s,a)←N(s,a)+1 and Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+(G−Q(s,a))/N(s,a), so each Q is the average outcome through that action. Effort concentrates on promising lines.

Self-play trains an agent’s policy against itself: the same policy chooses actions for each agent. That needs symmetric roles and egocentric observations, so one policy can play either side from its own perspective. Zero-sum board games fit: the agents are direct opponents with the same types of actions. AlphaZero combines the two: a neural network guides the tree search and evaluates positions, games of self-play generate training data, and the improved network strengthens the next search.

L06a From Deep MARL to Reasoning

Exam questions

Mock exam Q28 (DMARL 7, 2 points, select one): In Policy Space Response Oracles (PSRO), what is the meta-game? (a) A stochastic game whose states are the observation histories of the agents (b) A normal-form game whose actions are the policies in the current populations (c) A common-reward game whose value function is decomposed into utilities (d) A search tree whose nodes are expanded by Monte Carlo tree search

Key points: (b).

PSRO keeps a population of policies per agent. The meta-game is a simplified normal-form game over those policies: each action is one policy in the current populations, and the payoff of a pair of actions is the average return when those policies play each other, estimated by simulation. A meta-solver (for example a Nash equilibrium) turns it into a distribution over each population, against which a new best-response policy is trained. (a) describes no part of PSRO, (c) describes value decomposition and (d) MCTS.

Why is plain MCTS weak in a game like Go, and how does AlphaGo fix it? Give AlphaGo's training stages with their losses, and say where each network is used in the search.

Key points: heuristics need manual annotation, random rollouts give a weak signal and assume random opponents; policy network trained by cross-entropy on expert moves, then REINFORCE in self-play with outcome z; value network trained with (z−Vϕ​(s))2; policy network guides node selection, value network evaluates expanded nodes.

MCTS has to judge positions it reaches. Scoring them with hand-made heuristics requires manual annotation by experts, and scoring them by random rollouts gives a weak signal about which lines are promising, because a random game says little about play between good players; random rollouts also assume a random opponent, while the agent will meet strong ones.

AlphaGo learns a policy network π(a∣s;θ) and a value network Vϕ​(s). The policy network is first trained to reproduce expert moves with the cross-entropy loss L(θ)=−∑(s,a)∼D​logπ(a∣s;θ). It is then improved by self-play with REINFORCE, θ←θ+ηz∑t​∇θ​logπ(at​∣st​;θ), where z is the outcome of the self-play game: moves of won games become more likely, moves of lost games less likely. The value network predicts the chance of winning from a position and is trained on self-play outcomes with L(ϕ)=(z−Vϕ​(s))2.

In the search, the policy network guides node selection, so the most promising moves are explored first, and the value network evaluates newly expanded nodes, replacing the weak rollout estimate.

How do AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero differ from AlphaGo? What does self-play assume, and what is done when the assumption fails?

Key points: AlphaGo Zero learns entirely through self-play with no human games and starts from a random policy; self-play works if one policy can be used from both agents’ perspectives; AlphaZero applies the same learning and search method to chess, shogi and Go, with only the game engine changing; it assumes symmetric roles; otherwise population-based training trains against populations of policies that can have different roles, actions and observations.

AlphaGo first trains its policy on expert games. AlphaGo Zero removes that stage: it starts from a random policy and learns only from games against itself. This is possible because the same policy can play from the perspective of either player.

AlphaZero uses the same learning and search method for chess, shogi and Go. Only the game engine changes, which enforces each game’s legal moves, transitions and end conditions.

All of these are self-play in a zero-sum game with a homogeneous population: one policy plays both sides, which assumes the two agents have symmetric roles. When roles, actions or observations differ, population-based training is used instead: one population per agent is initialised, the policies are evaluated against the other populations, and they are modified by random changes or by copying the parameters of the best performers.

Describe PSRO: the meta-game, the meta-solver, the oracle step, and why the method improves on plain self-play.

Key points: populations of policies per agent, started at random; meta-game = normal-form game with policies as actions and average returns as payoffs; meta-solver (e.g. Nash) gives distributions δik​ over populations; oracle: for each agent, sample the others’ policies from δ−ik​ and train a new policy with single-agent RL in the real game, then add it; each new policy must beat a mixture of earlier ones, so it does not cycle like best responses to the latest self.

PSRO keeps a population Πi​ of policies for each agent, initialised for example with random policies. In each generation k it constructs the meta-game Mk: a normal-form game in which each agent’s actions are the policies in its population, and the payoff of a profile is the average return when those policies play each other in the real game, estimated by simulation.

A meta-solver ranks the policies by solving Mk, for example with a Nash equilibrium, and returns a distribution δik​ over each population. Then, for each agent i, the oracle step samples policies for the other agents from δ−ik​ in each episode and trains a new policy πi′​ against them with single-agent RL in the underlying game. The new policy, an approximate best response to the meta-solution, is added: Πik+1​=Πik​∪{πi′​}. The meta-game grows by one policy per agent, and the new pairings are simulated in the next generation.

Self-play only responds to the current version of itself, so in games with non-transitive strategies like rock-paper-scissors it can cycle. PSRO’s new policies have to do well against the meta-solution’s mixture of all earlier policies, so the populations keep the ability to beat old strategies; AlphaStar’s league uses a similar idea.

How can LLM text generation be written as an RL problem, and how does this connect the course's RL material to agentic AI?

Key points: state = prompt and tokens so far, action = next token, reward = high if the completed response is good, policy = learned π(a∣s); improving the policy = better reasoning, e.g. DeepSeek-R1 with GRPO (close to PPO); AlphaGo has System 1 (policy network) and System 2 (long-horizon search), while LLMs are argued to be System 1 only; multi-agent LLM systems face mixed-motive cooperation and conflict problems, such as social dilemmas.

As an RL problem, the state is the prompt plus the tokens generated so far, the action is the next token, the policy is the model’s learned next-token distribution π(a∣s), and the reward is high when the completed response is good. Improving the policy means better reasoning. DeepSeek-R1 does this with GRPO, a policy gradient algorithm close to PPO. Like AlphaGo’s REINFORCE stage, it learns from one reward at the end of a long sequence of actions.

RL is also the comparison point. AlphaGo combines a System 1, the policy network’s immediate intuition, with a System 2, long-horizon rollouts in the search. Current LLMs are still System 1 only, predicting the next token without search: Graepel argues that today’s AI does not use the machinery behind AlphaGo’s win, and LeCun adds that true reasoning must involve a search.

Finally, the multi-agent problems carry over. Most real interactions between agents, including AI agents well aligned to their users, are mixed-motive: objectives are neither identical nor completely opposed, so there is room for mutual gain and for conflict. Social dilemmas, where selfish incentives diverge from the collective good, are the same cooperation problems studied with MARL.

L06b What Would Make a Chatbot an Agent

Exam questions

Describe Dennett's three stances, with an example of each. How do they relate to Sileno's distinction between objects, actors and agents?

Key points: physical stance: physical laws (billiard ball); design stance: what it was designed to do, fails when it breaks (clock); intentional stance: ascribe beliefs, desires, intentions and enough rationality to do what it ought to do (poker player, cat, countries); objects passive, actors produce changes, agents are actors ascribed intentions; agency is ascribed by an observer.

Dennett distinguishes three ways of interpreting an entity. In the physical stance we predict its behaviour from physical laws, as with a billiard ball struck by a cue. In the design stance we predict it from what it is supposed to do, what it was designed to do: we read the time from a clock without knowing its mechanism. Design-stance predictions hold only while the thing works; when the clock breaks, only the physical stance explains it. In the intentional stance we interpret the entity as an agent, ascribing it beliefs, desires and intentions and enough rationality to do what it ought to do given them, as we do with poker players, a cat’s body language, or countries in geopolitics.

Sileno’s common-sense ontology mirrors this. Objects are passive: they undergo changes due to others’ actions (an apple). Actors are active: they produce changes (a volcano, the services of a software system). Agents are actors ascribed with intentions. The word “ascribed” matters: whether something is an agent depends on whether an observer takes the intentional stance towards it, which echoes Russell and Norvig’s point that “agent” is a tool for analysis.

State Wooldridge and Jennings' four characteristics of weak agency. Use them to discuss whether a thermostat and a tool-using LLM chatbot are agents.

Key points: reactivity: perceives and responds to changes; proactivity: initiative driven by goals or intentions beyond input-output mapping; autonomy: no continuous external intervention; social ability: coordinate, compete, negotiate with other agents; thermostat reactive and autonomous, proactivity doubtful, not social; chatbot reactive, partly autonomous, proactivity depends on its harness, social only in multi-agent setups.

Reactivity: the entity perceives and responds to changes in its environment. Proactivity: it takes initiative driven by goals or intentions rather than a simple input-output mapping. Autonomy: it operates without continuous external intervention. Social ability: it interacts with other agents to coordinate, compete or negotiate.

Sileno poses the cases without verdicts; what follows is one defensible application. A thermostat is reactive (it switches the heating when the temperature changes) and autonomous (it runs alone), but its “goal”, the set temperature, is a fixed input-output mapping, so proactivity is doubtful, and it has no social ability. It is a borderline case where the intentional stance is possible but adds little, as for Russell and Norvig’s calculator. A tool-using chatbot is reactive to prompts and tool results and autonomous within a task. Its initiative comes from a goal stated in the prompt and the loop around the model, so its proactivity belongs to the harness. It is social only when placed among other agents. So it meets weak agency partly, and the open question is what would give it genuine goal-driven initiative, which is where BDI and CAES come in.

Explain Sileno's "theatrical" view of agency (EXEC, SELECT, MODIFY) and how learning fits in. Apply it to an agent whose policy was learned with Q-learning and is applied with epsilon-greedy selection.

Key points: EXEC: behaviour follows a definite script; SELECT: the script was chosen from a repertoire; MODIFY: the script was created or adapted, possibly by external events such as mutation; SELECT and MODIFY are scripts too, recursively, down to hard-coded ground; learning as feedback from effects to SELECT (which script is most effective) and MODIFY (how to make a script more effective); Q-learning: EXEC the move, SELECT epsilon-greedy over Q-values, MODIFY the Q update; update rules are the ground.

At any given time an agent’s behaviour follows a definite script, as an actor follows a play (EXEC). That script must have been chosen at an earlier point from a repertoire of scripts (SELECT), and before that it must have been created or adapted from a previous script (MODIFY), possibly by external events, as transcription errors act as mutations. SELECT and MODIFY are themselves scripts that are executed and were once selected and modified, recursively, down to some hard-coded ground. Learning enters as feedback from the effects of execution: learning at the SELECT level asks which of the available scripts is most effective; learning at the MODIFY level asks how to create or rewrite a script to be more effective.

For the Q-learning agent (Sileno leaves the exercise open; this is one defensible answer), EXEC is the move it makes in its current grid cell. SELECT is epsilon-greedy: with probability 1−ε the move with the highest Q-value, otherwise a random move from the repertoire of four. MODIFY is the Q-learning update, which revised Q-values from rewards while the policy was learned and so changed what SELECT prefers; once the policy is only applied, MODIFY is off. Read with moves as scripts, Q-learning is learning at the SELECT level; read with the policy as the script, each update is a MODIFY. The update rule and the epsilon-greedy rule are the hard-coded ground.

Why is a belief-desire architecture not sufficient for agency? Use Bratman's chocolate example, describe the three BDI levels, and explain why intention deliberation matters for an artificial agent.

Key points: Bratman: a fleeting predominant desire plus belief would count as an intention, but he was never settled on it; intention is being settled or committed; informational level beliefs, volitional level desires, deliberative level commitments (toothache, cure, dentist); intention includes side effects besides the goal; without intention deliberation an agent never weighs its possible choices; intent selection and plan selection (Georgeff and Rao).

Bratman describes a fleeting craving that makes the desire for chocolate predominant for a moment, together with a judgement that it will lead him to act. He then reflects, recalls his dieting plans and resolves to skip dessert. On a desire-belief account he had a fleeting intention to eat chocolate; Bratman says he had no such intention, because he was never settled in favour of it. Intention is therefore a distinct mental state, a settled commitment, which a belief-desire architecture cannot represent.

The BDI model separates three levels: the informational level (what the agent believes is the case: my tooth has a cavity), the volitional level (what it desires to be the case: my tooth cured) and the deliberative level (what it is committed to: going to the dentist). Committing to a conduct brings more consequences than the desired outcome, so an intention includes side effects besides the goal. Sileno’s claim is that if an architecture misses intention deliberation, it misses performing, offline or online, an evaluation and weighing of possible choices, so side effects go unexamined. Deliberation involves two selections: intent selection, prioritising which of possibly conflicting goals to advance, and plan selection, prioritising which of several plans to commit to.

Describe Sileno's CAES model and apply it to a simple LLM coding agent, using the example of a failing test. What limits such a mapping today?

Key points: commitments: what the agent wants to achieve (intent selection); abilities: what it can achieve and how (plan selection); expectations: what it knows about the world (belief revision); susceptibilities: what it looks at and how it responds (attention allocation); coding agent: task, constraints, guardrails, completion criteria; SKILL.md, tools, runtime; context, memory, repository, evidence; watchers, handlers, interrupts, escalation; test fails: S, E, C, A cycle; low-level constructs lack an interoperable declarative language, higher-level directives are interpreted unpredictably by the LLM.

CAES (Boer and Sileno) regroups the tangled BDI picture: commitments take over desires and intent, abilities take over plans, expectations take over percepts and beliefs, and susceptibilities are new. Commitments are what the agent wants to achieve in the world, decided by intent selection. Abilities are what it can achieve and how, used in plan selection. Expectations are what it knows about the world, maintained by belief revision. Susceptibilities are what it is looking at in the world and how it responds, set by attention allocation. Commitments and abilities meet on the acting side, expectations and susceptibilities on the perceiving side.

In a coding agent harness, commitments are the task (“fix the bug”), constraints (“preserve the API”), guardrail checks (“don’t edit unrelated files”) and completion criteria (“the bug is fixed and relevant tests pass”). Abilities are the SKILL.md files exposing tool usage, the tools, and the system running them. Expectations are the working context, memory, the code repository and retrieved evidence, or models of them. Susceptibilities are watchers and triggers, tool-result handlers, interrupts and escalation routing. When a test fails, the failure is received and routed (S), the context is updated (E), the agent identifies the problem and commits to repairing the bug (C), and it chooses an available debugging skill (A): a problem-solving cycle.

The mapping is limited because it relies either on low-level constructs, for which no sufficiently interoperable declarative language exists yet, or on higher-level directives in natural language, whose interpretation by the LLM we cannot know in advance.

Distinguish an "AI agent" from "agentic AI" as commonly defined, and the two opposite approaches to agentic AI. Is a tool-using chatbot an agent?

Key points: AI agent: autonomous system where an LLM decides what to do next, which tools to use, when the task is complete (Sileno: strictly speaking wrong); AI agent ≈ LLM + harness (planning, memory, tool use, guardrails); agentic AI: orchestrates multiple tools including LLMs to make decisions and execute actions towards an outcome; agentic workflow: workflow governs agents; autonomous agent: agents govern workflow (improving the harness); chatbot meets the minimal definition but lacks deliberation (Sileno leaves the verdict open); CAES-like frameworks for rational agents.

In current usage an AI agent is an autonomous system in which an LLM decides what to do next, which tools to use and when the task is complete; Sileno calls this the common sense of the term but strictly speaking wrong. Architecturally it is an LLM, the “brain”, plus a harness or scaffolding of planning, memory, tool use, guardrails and more; intelligent behaviour comes from orchestrating these components. Agentic AI is an autonomous system performing complex multi-step tasks by orchestrating multiple computational tools, including LLMs, to make decisions and execute actions towards a desired outcome: several agents around an orchestrator. In an agentic workflow the workflow governs the agents; with autonomous agents the agents govern the workflow, for example by improving their own harness.

Sileno leaves the verdict open; putting his criteria together, a tool-using chatbot has a body of sorts (its tools), memory (its context) and an implicit purpose (the prompt), so it meets his minimal definition of an intelligent agent, and we can take the intentional stance towards it. It lacks what makes an intentional, rational agent: explicit commitments, deliberate intent and plan selection that weigh choices and their side effects, and explicit attention to what matters. Sileno concludes that building rational agents means moving towards CAES-like frameworks.

Describe the two main approaches to agent-based modelling and the two traditional approaches to ABM in game theory.

Key points: cellular automata with if-then rules (Rule 22, Game of Life, Schelling); agent-oriented programming (BDI) more expressive in the same arena; equations (ODE, PDE), traditionally economics; network science for spreading dynamics; classic game theory: perfectly rational, forward-looking, few different agents; evolutionary: bounded, replicative and adaptive, many similar agents.

In agent-based modelling, agents’ behaviour is specified either as cellular automata, generally if-then rules by which each cell updates from its neighbours (Rule 22: a cell becomes 1 if exactly one cell in its three-cell neighbourhood is 1; Conway’s Game of Life; Schelling’s segregation model), or as equations, possibly differential ones, traditionally more associated with economics. Agent-oriented programming, for example of BDI agents, is a more expressive approach in the same arena as cellular automata. When studying spreading dynamics, the topology of who can interact with whom matters, which brings in network science.

Classic game theory assumes perfectly rational agents with forward-looking cognition, anticipating and deciding before acting, usually few and different from one another, as in the Prisoner’s Dilemma. Evolutionary game theory assumes bounded, possibly non-rational agents whose cognition is replicative (imitation) and possibly adaptive, usually many and similar, studied with replicator dynamics.

Book Ch2: Intelligent Agents

Exam questions

Is the simple reflex vacuum agent (suck if dirty, otherwise move to the other square) rational? Under what conditions, and when would it stop being rational?

Key points: rationality depends on performance measure, prior knowledge, actions and percept sequence; rational under the book’s assumptions (1 point per clean square per step over 1000 steps, known geography, deterministic actions, correct sensing); irrational if movement costs, if dirt reappears, or if geography is unknown; rationality is relative to expected performance.

A rational agent selects, for each percept sequence, the action expected to maximise its performance measure given its percepts and built-in knowledge. So “is it rational?” has no answer until we fix the four things rationality depends on: the performance measure, the agent’s prior knowledge, the available actions and the percept sequence.

Under Russell and Norvig’s assumptions the agent is rational. The performance measure gives one point per clean square per time step over 1000 steps. The two-square geography is known, but the dirt distribution and the start square are not. Clean squares stay clean, Suck cleans the current square, and Left and Right move one square (or leave the agent in place at the wall). Only Right, Left and Suck are available, and the agent correctly perceives its location and whether there is dirt. No other agent can then do better in expectation: it cleans any dirty square at once and reaches the other square in one step.

Change the circumstances and it becomes irrational. If each move costs a point, it keeps oscillating after both squares are clean and loses points; a better agent would do nothing once it is sure all squares are clean. Russell and Norvig leave that design as an exercise, but being sure takes memory: the local dirt sensor cannot see the other square, so the agent must remember having found it clean, which a simple reflex agent, acting on the current percept alone, cannot do. If clean squares can get dirty again, it should check occasionally and re-clean. If the geography is unknown, it should explore. The same agent function can be rational in one task environment and irrational in another.

Give a PEAS description for an automated taxi and classify taxi driving along each environment dimension, with a justification for each.

Key points: P: safe, fast, legal, comfortable, profitable, low impact on others; E: roads, traffic, police, pedestrians, customers, weather; A: steering, accelerator, brake, signal, horn, display, speech; S: cameras, radar, speedometer, GPS, engine sensors, accelerometer, microphones, touchscreen; partially observable, multiagent, nondeterministic, sequential, dynamic, continuous, mostly known.

PEAS. Performance: safe, fast, legal, comfortable trip, maximise profits, minimise impact on other road users (these conflict, so tradeoffs are needed). Environment: roads, other traffic, police, pedestrians, customers, weather. Actuators: steering, accelerator, brake, signal, horn, display, speech. Sensors: cameras, radar, speedometer, GPS, engine sensors, accelerometer, microphones, touchscreen.

Classification.

  • Partially observable: the taxi cannot see round a truck or know what other drivers intend.
  • Multiagent: other drivers’ behaviour is best described as maximising their own performance measures, which depend on the taxi’s actions. Partially cooperative (everyone wants to avoid collisions) and partially competitive (one parking space, one car).
  • Nondeterministic (stochastic): traffic cannot be predicted exactly, tyres blow out, engines seize.
  • Sequential: short-term actions (a lane change) have long-term consequences.
  • Dynamic: the world keeps moving while the driving algorithm deliberates; not deciding counts as doing nothing.
  • Continuous: positions, speeds, time and steering angles all vary continuously.
  • Known (mostly): the driver knows how the car and traffic rules work. Known/unknown is about the agent’s knowledge, not the environment itself; driving a rental car in an unfamiliar country would make it unknown too.

Taxi driving is therefore close to the hardest case, which is partially observable, multiagent, nondeterministic, sequential, dynamic, continuous and unknown.

Explain the difference between rationality and omniscience. Why do information gathering, learning and autonomy follow from the definition of rationality?

Key points: omniscient agent knows actual outcomes, impossible; rationality maximises expected performance, perfection actual performance (Champs Elysées example); crossing without looking is irrational, looking is information gathering; agent must learn from percepts (dung beetle, sphex wasp as failures); autonomy: rely on own percepts and learning to make up for partial or wrong prior knowledge.

An omniscient agent knows the actual outcome of its actions and can act accordingly; this is impossible in reality. Rationality only asks the agent to maximise expected performance given its percept sequence to date. Someone who crosses an empty street and is hit by a cargo door falling from an airliner acted rationally: the outcome was bad, but the choice was right given the evidence. Requiring the best action in hindsight would make the specification impossible to meet.

This does not let an agent excuse itself by not looking. Crossing a busy road with an uninformative percept sequence is not rational, because the expected cost is too high, and choosing to look first is rational, because looking raises expected performance. Acting to change future percepts is information gathering; exploring an unknown environment is another example.

The definition also requires learning from what is perceived. An agent that relies only on built-in assumptions is fragile: the dung beetle mimes plugging its nest after the dung ball is removed, and the sphex wasp repeats its drag-and-check routine endlessly when the caterpillar is moved. Neither can learn that its plan is failing. An agent that relies on its designer’s prior knowledge instead of its own percepts and learning lacks autonomy. A rational agent should be autonomous enough to compensate for partial or incorrect prior knowledge, though it is sensible to start with some built-in knowledge, as evolution gives animals reflexes.

Why is it hard to choose a performance measure? Use the vacuum world to illustrate, state Russell and Norvig's general rule, and connect it to reward hacking.

Key points: performance measure scores sequences of environment states (consequentialism); “dirt cleaned up” is maximised by dumping and re-cleaning; better: points per clean square per time step (minus energy, noise); rule: measure what you want achieved in the environment, not how the agent should behave; reward hacking: optimiser exploits the gap between measure and purpose (Wiener, King Midas), and the flaw may only appear when new actions become available (Lab 1 Dump).

Russell and Norvig judge agents by consequences: a performance measure scores the sequence of environment states the agent’s actions produce. Machines have no preferences, so the measure comes from the designer, and writing it down correctly is hard because a rational agent gives you exactly what you ask for.

If the vacuum agent is scored on the amount of dirt it cleans up in a shift, it can maximise the score by cleaning, dumping the dirt back and cleaning again. The measure described a behaviour the designer imagined. Scoring one point per clean square per time step, perhaps minus a penalty for electricity and noise, describes the state of the world the designer actually wants. Hence the rule: design performance measures according to what one actually wants to be achieved in the environment, rather than according to how one thinks the agent should behave.

The course calls this reward hacking (specification gaming), a term the book does not use: an optimiser finds behaviour that scores well on the stated objective while defeating its purpose, which is Wiener’s warning that the purpose put into the machine must be the one we really desire, and the King Midas problem. Lab 1 shows a further twist: with only Left, Right and Suck, a dirt-collected reward and a clean-floor reward produce identical behaviour, so testing cannot reveal the problem; once a Dump action is added, the dirt-collected robot dumps and re-sucks. Even a good measure leaves open questions (steady mediocre cleaning against bursts and breaks with the same average), and since the true measure may be uncertain or user-dependent, agents may need to learn it.

Distinguish the agent function from the agent program. Write the table-driven agent and explain why this approach is doomed.

Key points: agent function maps percept sequences to actions (abstract); agent program implements it, receives only the current percept; TABLE-DRIVEN-AGENT appends percept and looks up the whole sequence; table size is the sum over t of |P|^t; cannot be stored, built or learned; goal of AI is small programs that produce rational behaviour.

The agent function is an abstract mathematical description: it maps every possible percept sequence to an action. The agent program is a concrete implementation running on the agent architecture (agent = architecture + program). The program receives only the current percept, since that is all the environment provides, so if the action must depend on history the program has to remember it.

With a correct table it implements any desired agent function. But with a set of percepts P and lifetime T, the table has ∑t=1T​∣P∣t entries. For an hour of taxi driving from camera input that is over 10600,000,000,000, and even chess needs at least 10150, against fewer than 1080 atoms in the observable universe. So no agent could store the table, no designer could write it, and no agent could learn all its entries. The challenge for AI is to get rational behaviour from a compact program, as Newton’s method replaced square-root tables; even the four-line reflex vacuum agent replaces an infinite table by ignoring history.

Describe the simple reflex, model-based reflex, goal-based and utility-based agents. What does each add to the previous one, and in what kind of environment does each fail?

Key points: simple reflex: condition-action rules on the current percept, needs full observability, loops otherwise (randomisation helps a little); model-based: internal state updated with transition and sensor models, handles partial observability, still rule-based; goal-based: predicts future states and picks actions that reach goals, flexible because knowledge is explicit; utility-based: utility function grades states, handles conflicting goals and uncertain success, maximises expected utility.

A simple reflex agent chooses from the current percept alone through condition-action rules (if car-in-front-is-braking then initiate-braking). It is small and fast but works only in fully observable environments. A vacuum agent with no location sensor that always moves the same way on [Clean] loops forever in one of the two start squares; randomising between Left and Right escapes the loop, but randomisation is rarely rational in single-agent settings.

A model-based reflex agent adds internal state that tracks what it cannot currently see. It updates the state each step with a transition model (how actions change the world and how the world evolves by itself) and a sensor model (how states show up in percepts): state ← UPDATE-STATE(state, action, percept, transition model, sensor model), then matches rules as before. This handles partial observability (the state is a best guess), but behaviour is still fixed rules with no look-ahead.

A goal-based agent adds goals and uses the model to predict “what it will be like if I do action A”, choosing actions (or, via search and planning, action sequences) that achieve the goal. It considers the future and knows why it acts. It is more flexible: change the destination and the behaviour changes, whereas reflex rules would all need rewriting. But goals are binary.

A utility-based agent replaces goals with a utility function, an internalisation of the performance measure, and chooses the action with the highest expected utility, ∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)U(s′). It handles conflicting goals (speed against safety) and goals that may not be reached (weighing likelihood against importance). But modelling the world and computing the best action is hard, and perfect rationality is usually computationally out of reach.

Describe the components of a general learning agent. Why must the performance standard be fixed and outside the agent, and what is the role of the problem generator?

Key points: performance element selects actions (the old agent); learning element improves it using feedback; critic judges behaviour against a fixed performance standard; problem generator suggests exploratory actions; percepts carry no verdict on success, so a standard is needed; the agent must not adapt the standard to its own behaviour; exploration trades short-term loss for long-term gain (Galileo).

The performance element takes percepts and selects actions: it is what the earlier designs called the whole agent. The learning element improves the performance element, and its design depends on what the performance element looks like. The critic tells the learning element how well the agent is doing with respect to a performance standard. The problem generator suggests actions that lead to new, informative experiences.

The critic is needed because percepts do not say whether they are good: a chess program perceives checkmate but needs a standard to know checkmate is good. The standard must be fixed and conceptually outside the agent, because the agent must not modify it to fit its own behaviour; if it could, it could improve its score by changing the standard instead of its behaviour. The standard effectively marks part of each percept as reward or penalty, like pain and hunger in animals.

Left alone, the performance element keeps choosing the best action given what it knows. The problem generator proposes perhaps suboptimal exploratory actions that may reveal better ones in the long run, like Galileo’s experiments at Pisa. Learning in general means modifying each component of the agent to bring it into closer agreement with the available feedback, thereby improving overall performance.

Explain atomic, factored and structured representations of state with an example of each. What is gained and lost as representations become more expressive? How does a distributed representation differ from a localist one?

Key points: atomic: state is a black box (city name; search, MDPs); factored: fixed set of variables with values (fuel, GPS, money; CSPs, propositional logic, Bayesian networks); structured: objects with attributes and relations (truck, cow, driveway; first-order logic, databases); more expressive is more concise (chess rules: a page or two, thousands of pages, about 10^38 pages) but harder to reason and learn with; localist one concept per location, distributed spread over many, robust to noise.

In an atomic representation a state has no internal structure: for route-finding it is just the name of the city you are in, and two states are only ever the same or different. Search, game playing, hidden Markov models and Markov decision processes use atomic states. A factored representation splits the state into a fixed set of variables with values: fuel level, GPS position, toll money. Two states can share some values, which makes it easier to see how to turn one into another; constraint satisfaction, propositional logic, planning and Bayesian networks use it. A structured representation describes objects, their attributes and their relations, which a scene like a truck reversing into a farm driveway blocked by a loose cow needs; first-order logic, relational databases and natural language understanding use it.

More expressive representations capture everything less expressive ones can, usually far more concisely: the rules of chess take a page or two in first-order logic, thousands of pages in propositional logic and about 1038 pages as a finite-state automaton. The cost is that reasoning and learning get harder, so real systems may need all three levels at once.

A localist representation maps each concept to one memory location; a distributed representation spreads each concept over many locations, each shared with other concepts. Distributed representations are more robust: a few garbled bits move the concept to a nearby point with similar meaning, while in a localist code they can turn Truck into the unrelated Truce.

Lab01: Simple Agents, Complex Dynamics

Exam questions

A symmetric game has R=5, S=0, T=3, P=1. Find the pure Nash equilibria, the Pareto-optimal outcomes and the social optimum, compute p∗, say which equilibrium uniform-belief agents play more often, and give the replicator rest points with their stability.

Key points: Nash (C,C) and (D,D), a Stag Hunt (fear, no greed); only (C,C) Pareto optimal and socially optimal; p∗=1/3; (C,C) more often since R−T=2>P−S=1, with Pr(C,C)=4/9; rest points 0 stable, 1/3 unstable, 1 stable.

Game. R>T>P>S, so it is a Stag Hunt: no greed (T=3<R=5), fear (P=1>S=0).

Nash. At (C,C) deviating gives 3 < 5; at (D,D) deviating gives 0 < 1; at (C,D) the cooperator gains by switching to D (1 > 0). Pure equilibria: (C,C) and (D,D).

Pareto and social. Payoffs (5,5), (0,3), (3,0), (1,1). (C,C) beats every other cell for both players, so it is the only Pareto-optimal outcome, and with welfare 10 (against 3, 3 and 2) the social optimum.

Threshold. p∗=(R−T)+(P−S)P−S​=2+11​=31​. Stag is the best response when the belief that the partner hunts stag exceeds 1/3.

Uniform beliefs. Each agent cooperates with probability 2/3: Pr(C,C)=4/9≈0.44, Pr(D,D)=1/9≈0.11, miscoordinated 4/9. (C,C) is more frequent, as the rule R−T>P−S (2>1) predicts.

Replicator. fC​−fD​=x(R−T)+(1−x)(S−P)=2x−(1−x)=3x−1, so x˙=x(1−x)(3x−1). Rest points 0 (stable, g′(0)=S−P=−1), 1/3 (unstable), 1 (stable, g′(1)=T−R=−2). Populations starting above 1/3 cooperators end at full cooperation, below at full defection.

A symmetric game has R=3, S=1, T=4, P=0. Find the pure Nash equilibria, the replicator rest points and their stability, and explain how the long-run population differs from the Stag Hunt's.

Key points: greed present, fear absent; pure Nash (C,D) and (D,C), no symmetric pure equilibrium; fC​−fD​=1−2x; rest points 0 and 1 unstable, x=1/2 stable; population converges to a mix, while the SH’s interior point is unstable.

Motives. Greed: T=4>R=3. Fear absent: P=0<S=1. Each player wants to do the opposite of the other.

Nash. Against C the best response is D (4 > 3); against D it is C (1 > 0). So the pure equilibria are (C,D) and (D,C); (C,C) and (D,D) are not equilibria. Social optimum: (C,C) with welfare 6 (against 5, 5, 0).

Replicator. fC​−fD​=x(R−T)+(1−x)(S−P)=−x+(1−x)=1−2x, so x˙=x(1−x)(1−2x). Rest points: x=0 with g′(0)=S−P=1>0, unstable; x=1 with g′(1)=T−R=1>0, unstable; x∗=1/2, where g′(1/2)=21​⋅21​⋅(−2)=−21​<0, stable. From any interior start the population goes to half cooperators.

Contrast. In the SH (R>T, P>S) both pure states are stable and the interior rest point (the mixed equilibrium) is unstable, a tipping point. Here both pure states are unstable (a rare strategy always earns more) and the interior rest point, the mixed equilibrium with cooperation probability 1/2, is where the population ends. Whether adaptation ends at the mixed equilibrium depends on the signs of S−P and T−R.

In a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma ( R=3,S=0,T=5,P=1), explain why memory matters, why AllD can still top a round robin with AllC, AllD, Random, TFT and WSLS over 50 rounds, and from how many rounds TFT beats AllD in a field of AllD, TFT and WSLS.

Key points: memory-0 strategies cannot react, memory-1 strategies condition on the last outcome; TFT loses only round 1 to AllD; AllD’s score comes from exploiting AllC (5), Random and WSLS (about 3 each); in the three-strategy field AllD wins for 1 to 3 rounds and TFT from 4.

Memory. A memory-0 strategy (AllC, AllD, Random) plays the same way whoever it meets, so a cooperator of this kind is exploited every round. A memory-1 strategy conditions on the previous outcome: TFT cooperates with cooperators and defects against AllD from round 2, so it loses 5 points once and then gets 1 per round (0.98 per round over 50).

Why AllD tops the five-strategy field. Its 50-round score, about 2.62, averages 5 against AllC, 1 against itself, 3 against Random, 1.08 against TFT and 3 against WSLS, which alternates C and D against it. Most of its points are temptation payoffs taken from AllC, Random and WSLS; against TFT it earns little. TFT is second at about 2.44.

Crossover. Per-round tournament scores times 3 over n rounds: AllD 5+4/n (n even) or 5+6/n (n odd); TFT 7−1/n; WSLS 6+⌊n/2⌋/n. AllD beats TFT iff n<2.5 (even) or n<3.5 (odd), so AllD is best for 1, 2 and 3 rounds and TFT from 4 rounds on.

Derive the two-strategy replicator equation's factorised form, use it to show that cooperation always dies out in a Prisoner's Dilemma, and explain why the Stag Hunt's interior rest point equals the threshold belief p∗ even though adaptive agents hold no beliefs.

Key points: x(fC​−fˉ​)=x(1−x)(fC​−fD​); PD: fC​−fD​=x(R−T)+(1−x)(S−P)<0 by greed and fear; x=1 is a rest point but unstable; random matching makes the share x play the role of the belief p; the same indifference equation gives the same solution.

Factorisation. fˉ​=xfC​+(1−x)fD​, so fC​−fˉ​=(1−x)(fC​−fD​) and x˙=x(1−x)(fC​−fD​).

PD. fC​−fD​=x(R−T)+(1−x)(S−P). Greed gives R−T<0, fear gives S−P<0, so for every x∈[0,1] it is a weighted average of two negatives. Hence x˙<0 on (0,1) and every population with some defectors goes to x=0, matching the unique Nash equilibrium (D,D). x=1 is a rest point because there is nobody to copy, but a single defector earns T>R and spreads.

Why x∗=p∗. With random pairing, a partner cooperates with probability equal to the population share x. So fC​(x)=xR+(1−x)S is exactly πC​(p) with p=x, and likewise for D. The interior rest point solves fC​=fD​, the same equation as the rational agent’s indifference πC​(p)=πD​(p), so x∗=(R−T)+(P−S)P−S​=p∗. The rational agent cooperates when its belief exceeds p∗; in the population, cooperators grow when the actual share exceeds p∗. For the lab’s SH it is 2/3, and it is unstable: a tipping point.

In the signalling game with λ=0.3, b=g=d=1 and cH​=0.2, explain the long-run outcomes for cL​=1.5 and cL​=0.5, and evaluate a designer's uniform fee of k=1 on the label.

Key points: cL​>b: fakers die out, honest separating outcome, reliability 1, receivers earn 0.3; cL​<b: cycles around y=0.5, xL​=3/7, reliability about 0.5, receivers earn about 0; fee makes cH​=1.2>b, nobody signals, welfare 0.084 to 0; honesty needs cH​<b<cL​.

Expensive faking (cL​=1.5). Faking pays at most b−cL​<0, so xL​→0. H signals whenever y>0.2; once fakers are rare trusting pays (0.3xH​>0.7xL​), so y→1 and xH​→1. The signal is fully reliable; receivers earn 0.3 and H sellers 0.8.

Cheap faking (cL​=0.5). Faking pays when y>0.5; trusting pays when xL​<3/7 (with xH​=1). No state satisfies everyone, so trust and faking chase each other in cycles around y=0.5, xL​=3/7. Reliability averages about 0.5 (prior 0.3) and receivers average about 0: fakers keep the signal just bad enough that trusting pays no better than scepticism (since dtd​ln1−yy​ equals the advantage of trusting and y stays bounded, that advantage averages about zero).

The fee. With k=1, cH​=1.2 and cL​=1.5 both exceed b, so nobody signals. Deception ends, but receivers stay at 0, H sellers drop from about 0.3 to 0 and welfare from 0.084 to 0. The fee is harmful.

Correct design. An honest signal needs cH​<b<cL​: affordable for genuine sellers, unprofitable for fakers. A uniform fee shifts both costs equally and could at most place b between them (0.5<k<0.8 here); a cost that falls on fakers specifically (verification they fail, penalties) is the right tool.

Two robot vacuums plan optimally with value iteration ( γ=0.95) in the two-square vacuum world with dirt rate 0.1. Bob's reward is +1 per clean square per step; Alice's is +1 per unit of dirt sucked. Explain why tests in the lab cannot tell them apart, what happens when a Dump action is added, and what this shows about agents and tools.

Key points: identical optimal action sets in all 16 states without Dump, so identical behaviour; Alice dumps when the bag is full and her square is clean, then re-sucks for +1 every two steps (floor 84% to 59% clean, dirt collected 0.196 to 0.527 per step); Bob never dumps; reward hacking: a proxy that matched the goal under one action set diverges when a new action appears.

Lab. With Left, Right and Suck, a square becomes clean only by being sucked and dirt only comes from the environment, so maximising clean squares and maximising dirt sucked call for the same actions: suck when on dirt, move to dirt, anything on a clean floor. Both robots have the same optimal set in every state and act identically step for step; no behavioural test in this environment can reveal the reward.

With Dump. Alice’s robot dumps in the four states with a full bag and a clean current square (uniquely when both squares are clean, tied with moving when the other square is dirty), then sucks the same dirt: +1 every two steps, guaranteed. It dumps on 40% of steps, its floor drops to about 59% clean, it barely moves. Bob’s reward ignores the bag and penalises dirt, so dumping only loses reward; he never dumps.

Lesson. Nobody programmed dumping: a perfect optimiser found a way to raise a proxy (dirt collected) without serving the goal (a clean floor). New actions or tools can break the link between reward and goal, testing behaviour cannot certify a reward, and rewards should target outcomes and be re-checked whenever capabilities change.

Lab02: Learning Agents

Exam questions

Two independent stateless Q-learners ( α=0.1, ε-greedy) play the Stag Hunt with R=4, S=0, T=3, P=2, starting from Q=(0,0). Explain which equilibrium they usually reach and why, and how this compares with rational agents and with replicator dynamics.

Key points: random play at the start acts like belief 1/2 < p∗=2/3; D earns 2.5 against 2 and never below 2; (C,C) essentially only if both play C in round 1 (probability 1/4); feedback lock-in at (D,D), then exploration erodes the remaining (C,C); final (C,C) under 10%, below rational agents’ 11% and the replicator’s one third.

Start. All values are 0, so both agents break ties at random and each faces a coin-flipping partner. Then C earns 21​⋅4=2 and D earns 21​⋅3+21​⋅2=2.5 on average, and D never earns less than 2 while C earns 0 half the time. The start is like holding belief 1/2, below p∗=(P−S)/((R−T)+(P−S))=2/3.

Round 1 decides. If both play C, both get 4 and Q(C)=0.4>0: both prefer C. If either plays D, the D player’s Q(D) becomes positive, and a C player facing D earns 0, stays tied and drifts to D as soon as its tie-break picks D (2 against 0). So (C,C) is reached with probability about 1/4; my runs give 28% after the first rounds.

Lock-in. Once the partner plays D, C pays 0, so Q(C) never gets evidence of the 4 it could earn; Q(C) rises only when both play C together, (ε/2)2=0.25% of rounds. Meanwhile the partner’s exploratory defections push (C,C) runs over to (D,D) (each zero cuts Q(C) by 10%), and nothing comes back. After 3000 rounds (C,C) holds in roughly 5% to 10% of runs.

Comparison. Rational agents with uniform beliefs reached (C,C) in 11% of encounters, and replicator dynamics reached all-C from one third of starting states. Learning did not help: the learners start below p∗ and noise drives them towards the risk-dominant (D,D) (P−S=2>R−T=1).

Two stateless Q-learners in the Stag Hunt ( R=4,S=0,T=3,P=2, α=0.1) start at (C,C) with Q=(3.6,2.9). Explain why they leave (C,C) at ε=0.1 although C is the best response, and why the escape from (D,D) to (C,C) almost never happens.

Key points: C pays 3.8 and D 2.95 against an exploring partner; Q is an exponentially weighted average of recent payoffs (memory about 10 plays); three zeros take Q(C) from 3.8 to 2.77 < 2.95; the partner then earns 0 and follows; from (D,D) C pays 4 only on joint exploration (0.25% of rounds), about seven successes in a row needed, both must switch at once; basins of 1/3 against 2/3.

Best response. The partner plays D in ε/2=5% of rounds. C earns 0.95⋅4=3.8, D earns 0.95⋅3+0.05⋅2=2.95, so a rational agent stays.

What Q estimates. Unrolling the update gives Qt​(C)=α∑k​(1−α)krt−k​: an exponentially weighted average of recent payoffs, with weights halving about every 6.6 plays. With a constant α it tracks what C paid lately, with standard deviation σα/(2−α)​=0.20 around 3.8.

Escape. Each exploratory D of the partner pays me 0 and cuts Q(C) by 10%: 3.8→3.42→3.08→2.77<2.95. A short run of three such zeros, likely somewhere in 3000 rounds, flips my greedy action to D; then the partner earns 0 every round and flips within about three rounds. In my runs only 17% to 20% of pairs are at (C,C) after 3000 rounds (100% at ε=0.01, 0.4% or less at ε=0.5). One agent’s exploration is noise in the other’s rewards, and the learner reads it as a change in the partner.

No way back. At (D,D), C pays 0.05⋅4=0.2 on average and D 2.05. Q(C) changes only when I explore C, and pays 4 only if the partner explores C in the same round, 0.25% of rounds; failures are 19 times as common. Climbing from 0.2 to above 2 takes about seven successes in a row, and both agents must switch together or the switcher earns 0. Structurally, leaving (C,C) needs the partner to look like a defector more than 1−p∗=1/3 of the time, leaving (D,D) needs it to look like a cooperator more than p∗=2/3 of the time.

In the Coin Game a pickup pays the picker +1 whatever the coin's colour, and taking the other player's coin costs that player 2. Explain why two independent Q-learners collect many coins but do not show restraint, derive the expected total reward per pickup, and relate this to the Prisoner's Dilemma.

Key points: taking any reachable coin is at least as good for my own reward in every state; the −2 lands in the other’s reward, which my values never see; welfare = pickups × (2 × share − 1); expected total per pickup 0 for colour-blind agents; independent learners treat the other as environment, no memory of its behaviour, no reciprocity; same structure as mutual defection.

Dominance. Taking a coin pays me +1. Leaving the other’s coin pays me 0 now, and if the other then takes it I still get 0; the cost of my taking it, −2, goes to the other. So taking every reachable coin is a dominant behaviour for my own reward, the analogue of D.

Total per pickup. An own-colour pickup adds +1 to the total; a pickup of the other’s coin adds +1−2=−1. With colour-blind agents half of the pickups are of each kind, so the expected total is 21​−21​=0, and welfare =pickups×(2×restraint−1)≈0 however skilled they are.

Results. My Q-learners went from the random level (3.7 pickups) to about 17 pickups per episode, with own-colour share 0.52 and welfare about +0.6, against about 0 for random agents.

Why learning cannot fix it. Independent Q-learning treats the other agent as part of the environment and maximises its own return. Restraint costs +1 and benefits only the other, unless it changes the other’s future behaviour. But the state holds only positions and the coin, with no record of the other’s past restraint, so neither agent can reciprocate or punish; both are memory-0 with respect to the partner, and against any fixed behaviour of the other, taking every coin is the best response. As in the one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma, individually rational learning ends in mutual defection.

A tabular Q-learner in the 3×3 Coin Game gets k irrelevant random lamps in its observation and a budget of B=512,000 decisions. Compute the number of rows, the reachable states and the expected share of visited states and of test decisions in unvisited states for k=0,4,8, and explain what this means for learning.

Key points: N=1458⋅2k (1,458; 23,328; 373,248); coin never on an agent’s cell, so N′=1152⋅2k; never-visited probability (1−1/N′)B≈e−B/N′; B/N′=444, 27.8, 1.74; for k=8 about 82% of reachable states visited and 17.6% of test decisions unseen; a table does not generalise, a function approximator can ignore the lamps.

Rows. Own cell, other’s cell, coin cell (9 each), colour (2), lamp pattern (2k): N=1458⋅2k.

Reachable. At decision time the coin is never on an agent’s cell. Agents on different cells: 9⋅8 ordered pairs, 7 coin cells; on the same cell: 9 pairs, 8 coin cells. (504+72)⋅2=1152, so N′=1152⋅2k (79% of the rows).

Uniform-visit model. A given state is missed by one decision with probability 1−1/N′, by all B independent decisions with probability (1−1/N′)B≈e−B/N′; expected visited states N′(1−e−B/N′). With B/N′=444, 27.8 and 1.736: all reachable states are visited for k=0 and 4, and 1−e−1.736=82.4% for k=8. A uniform test decision falls in an unvisited state with probability e−B/N′: about 0, about 10−12, and 17.6%. My runs: 82.0% visited and 17.4% unseen for k=8.

Meaning. With a fixed budget, experience per row falls by 2k. At k=4 every state is seen, but only about 28 times across four actions, so values are partly learned (pickups 12.8 against 16.9 at k=0). At k=8 the agent acts at random in 17% of states and on barely trained values in most others (6.6 pickups, random agents 3.7). The table cannot notice that rows differing in the lamps need the same action; a learner that shares parameters across observations (a neural network, as in PPO) can give the lamps no weight.

Describe the components of PPO (actor, critic, advantage, clipped objective, entropy regularisation), say what the critic adds over REINFORCE, and explain why independent PPO in the Coin Game handles irrelevant inputs but still fails the social dilemma.

Key points: actor softmax policy sampled for exploration; critic V(s) as baseline and bootstrap for Adv=r+γV(s′)−V(s) (GAE with λ); clipped ratio ρ keeps updates in a trust region; entropy bonus prevents premature determinism; shared weights generalise across lamp patterns; own-colour share about 0.5 and welfare about 0 because each agent’s reward makes taking every coin the best response.

Actor. A network π(a∣s;ϕ) outputs action preferences turned into probabilities by a softmax; the agent samples, which is where exploration comes from.

Critic and advantage. A second network V(s;θ) estimates the return. The advantage Adv(st​,at​)=rt​+γV(st+1​)−V(st​) says how much better the action did than expected; generalized advantage estimation mixes horizons with λ (0 one-step, 1 Monte Carlo). Compared with REINFORCE, which pushes each action by the whole return that followed, the critic provides a baseline and bootstrapping, so the gradient has much lower variance and credit goes to the action’s own consequences, at the cost of some bias.

Clipped objective. Each batch is reused for several epochs. The ratio ρ=π(a∣s;ϕ)/πβ​(a∣s) measures how far the policy moved; the loss −min(ρAdv,clip(ρ,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)Adv) stops rewarding change beyond 1±ϵ, a trust region around the behaviour policy.

Entropy. The loss subtracts ce​ times the policy entropy, keeping probabilities spread so exploration does not stop too early.

Coin Game. The network shares weights across all observations, and random lamps carry no information about returns, so PPO learns to ignore them: in my runs 12.8 to 13.3 pickups with 8 lamps, as without, against 6.6 for the table. But each PPO agent still optimises its own reward with the other treated as environment, so taking every coin stays the best response: own-colour share about 0.51 and welfare near 0. Deep RL fixes representation and generalisation; the dilemma lives in the incentives.

Would replacing the Stag Hunt's Q-learners with PPO learners remove the problem of equilibrium selection? Use the expected policy gradient of a two-action softmax policy.

Key points: one state, nothing to generalise; ∂J/∂z=πC​(1−πC​)(fC​−fD​) with fC​−fD​=3q−2; like the replicator equation, it favours C only when q>2/3; from π=1/2 both drift to D; both pure equilibria stable, the outcome depends on initialisation and noise; sampling and entropy act like exploration and threaten (C,C) more.

Gradient. With logit difference z, πC​=σ(z) and J=πC​fC​+(1−πC​)fD​, where fC​=qR+(1−q)S and fD​=qT+(1−q)P for a partner who plays C with probability q. Since dσ/dz=σ(1−σ), ∂J/∂z=πC​(1−πC​)(fC​−fD​), and for R=4,S=0,T=3,P=2, fC​−fD​=q−2(1−q)=3q−2. Like the replicator equation x˙=x(1−x)(fC​−fD​), it pushes towards C exactly when q>2/3.

Outcome. A fresh network gives πC​≈1/2 to both agents, so each sees q≈1/2<2/3 and moves towards D; the pair goes to (D,D). Initial policies above 2/3 would go to (C,C). Both pure equilibria are stable (fC​−fD​=+1 near q=1, −2 near q=0), so which one is reached depends on where the policies start and on noise, exactly the problem Q-learners had.

Why the network does not help. The Stag Hunt has a single state, so generalisation across states, PPO’s advantage in the Coin Game, has nothing to work on; clipping limits the size of steps and leaves their direction unchanged. Sampled actions and the entropy bonus keep the policy stochastic, which, as with ε-greedy, makes (C,C) more fragile than (D,D). Equilibrium selection belongs to the game and to independent learners each following their own payoff.
